# Junior delegation protocol

The full protocol referenced from `SKILL.md`'s "Gates worth remembering" section — decided from the
request, BEFORE the first tool call (SPEC INV-69).

**Junior delegation (decided from the request, BEFORE the first tool call):** the trigger is judgment
against mechanical — work whose steps can be written precisely (known edit strings, a known command,
fan-out fact-gathering, a report or list or dump to produce) routes to a worker, while anything carrying
judgment or design stays senior. Size is a weak hint only, never the decider. The trigger, the tier
ladder, and the raw-output law all live in the base skill's rule 5 and the routing rule — this passage is
their reference; it is not a second home (live-spec-base rule 5, SPEC INV-69).

**The routing rule (SPEC INV-69) picks the tier — propose the cheapest tier that can pass the brief, the
senior may overrule it aloud:** the proposal reads the STEP and kind of the work, beyond the row's size
alone — a judgment step (spec, prove, architecture, matrix-level calls, findings triage, any taste call)
proposes the senior and is never routed down, a mechanical step proposes a worker at the tier above. The
economy rung moves the threshold (at `lean` an airtight brief rides one tier cheaper, at `tight` the
cheapest sufficient tier is always the proposal). And the proposal is ADVISORY — the senior may override
per wish, the override logged as one line on the checkpoint and the delivery report, proposed tier → chosen
tier → why.

**The brief is self-contained (the BMAD story-file lesson):** delegated work ships as one document
embedding the EXACT spec sentences it serves, the exact edit strings or commands, the checks to run, and
the checkpoint path — the worker never hunts context, never interprets the spec, never decides. If writing
the brief means deciding something first, that decision is the senior's and happens BEFORE delegation —
"explaining it would take longer than doing it" is how delegation silently dies.

**The brief's birth has three laws (SPEC INV-53/54/55):** a brief that edits existing files is born from
READING them in full — three recorded lines per file (current state · what changes · what must survive),
every step back-referencing its spec sentence, every technical claim citing a source (a file:line, a
command's output), never memory of a file. The brief carries the closed HALT list — ambiguous requirement
· two consecutive unexplained failures of one command · missing config/dependency · acceptance impossible
as briefed — stop WITH evidence, otherwise run to completion (the senior's escalation ladder is a separate
move, after a failed acceptance). And the brief is SIZED — its text within ~300 lines, at most ~8 files to
edit [default], the work splitting above either — passing PATHS, never inlined file bodies. See the private
playbook repo's PLAYBOOK.md.

**The worker contract (SPEC ACT-3):** the brief NAMES the files the worker may write — its session's
write-ownership narrowed to exactly those, reads free, writes fenced. Same-session sibling-worker files
are fence-benign (the concurrent-edit fence alarms on foreign sessions, staying quiet on your own briefed
hands — the senior who briefed both owns the seams between briefs). Owning those seams is a brief-time
act: before spawning another concurrent writer, the senior confirms its brief's write-set is disjoint
from every already-running writer's brief, or gives it an isolated worktree (SPEC INV-105) — because
the fence stays silent between same-session siblings, this disjointness is settled when the briefs are
written, ahead of the new worker's first write. The session's live setting lines ride
into the brief verbatim — a worker never resolves the settings ladder itself, it cannot hear the human's
spoken word.

**A worker never restores a working tree with a git command (SPEC INV-298; the gate INV-299).** Before a worker
mutates a file it means to put back, it reads that file and holds its bytes. A worker puts a file
back by WRITING ITS OWN SAVED BYTES. A worker runs no command that discards uncommitted work, in any
tree: `git checkout -- <path>`, `git checkout .`, `git restore` outside `--staged`, `git stash` and
its `push`, `save`, `create` and `store` forms, `git reset` with `--hard`, `--merge` or `--keep`, and
`git clean` with `-f` or `-x`. Such a command's blast radius is a PATH, so its damage lands on files
the worker never wrote and its brief never named. This rule binds a worker in every tree, including
its own isolated worktree, since a worktree shares one repository with the lanes beside it and a
worker cannot read off its brief what else that repository holds. A worker that holds no saved bytes
for a file it mutated, or that believes a file needs a git-level restore, HALTS and reports the file
and the mutation it made, and it writes no further file and runs no further command. The
orchestrator owns recovery: it restores the named file from the last committed stage, hands the
worker a fresh brief carrying that file's current bytes, and records the halt in the row's delivery
report, and the halted work resumes under that new brief. The orchestrator's own half: a finished
build stage is committed before the next worker touches its files, so a worker that hits a broken
file has a commit to be recovered from. `guardrails/check-worker-restore.py` reads the worker runs'
transcripts for the command and runs at the verify step. The write-set disjointness above fences
EDITS and gives no cover here, which is why the clause stands on its own: the two destructions of
uncommitted work on 2026-07-23 and the near miss of 2026-07-27 all came from a worker running
correct-looking work, and the `git status` it pasted afterwards read "clean" in the safe case and the
destructive one alike. The clause rides every brief this protocol composes.

**The brief carries the register laws, so the worker's own text obeys them (SPEC INV-221, INV-173).** The
brief states the register laws the worker's report and any agent-to-agent message must hold — the
no-scissors law (no naming a thing by denying its neighbour, SPEC INV-173) and the no-dramatization law
(grading the size of a change, up or down, is the reader's act, SPEC INV-221). A worker writes text a
human reads, and the chat and document judges [INV-203] never read its report, so the brief is where the
laws reach it. The worked instance: workers reporting to this pack opened "Excellent work" and named a
premise wrong "in an important way", both graded-size sentences the worker had no brief telling it to
drop (the owner's count, 2026-07-17).

The brief ARMS the worker for the workshop — it carries the host's problem-ledger path
(`.live-spec/PROBLEMS.md`) with the WATCHED-line duty: workshop noise the worker hits (a flaky harness, a
missing dependency, a tool misbehaving) goes into its checkpoint as a ledger line — signature, date, one
line of context, logged every time — and the senior carries the lines into the ledger at verify (SPEC
INV-23). And it carries the CLOCK — the date and time read at briefing — so the worker stamps its
checkpoint and any dated output from the brief's clock, never an invented hour (SPEC INV-24; a worker WITH
a shell re-reads the machine clock itself — the brief's line is the floor for one without, and elapsed
time is never guessed). And a result failing its brief's acceptance escalates exactly ONE tier every time,
with a logged line covering the move — one rung up, in order, always logged.

**Every delegation reports its saving:** the
delivery report carries one line — what went to the worker and roughly how much senior work it saved.
The line is what keeps the habit alive; a session that never writes it is a session that quietly
stopped delegating. The line lives in the row's delivery report, which the closing commit moves to the archive with the
row, and a suite check reads it from the archive: a delivered row without the line goes red
(SPEC INV-103, INV-276, forward from 2026-07-12).
 The same accounting also names the reads dispatched beside the work delegated, so a session that filled its own context with a read it should have dispatched shows that in the report (SPEC INV-137). Each work block in the report opens by naming its root, and the report accounts the block against its announced plan line (SPEC INV-314). The duty binds the
orchestrator seat regardless of model, whatever tier leads the seat.

1	# The excuses table
2	
3	The shortcuts that break the method never announce themselves; they arrive as one of these thoughts.
4	Each is a tripwire: thinking it means STOP and take the pipeline door you were about to skip.
5	
6	| The thought | Why it is a trap |
7	|---|---|
8	| "it's a one-liner / just a prototype" | The Room was "just to see" — it shipped hover-only with no phone layout and no spec. Size never picks the door; the tripwires do (base rule 15). |
9	| "I'll write the spec after it works" | Spec-after-code documents what you built, apart from what was asked; the prover can no longer catch the difference (spec-author anti-pattern). |
10	| "the human is in a hurry" | Urgency moves PRIORITY, never the door — a critical feature heads the queue, it still enters at the spec step (SPEC T-12). |
11	| "the suite is green, ship it" | Green proves the facts the matrix knows; an unspecced surface has no rows, so green says nothing about it (SPEC INV-15). |
12	| "asking would bother them" | Batched questions exist exactly for this; a silent guess costs a re-build, the batch costs one read (SPEC INV-4, INV-5). |
13	| "explaining it would take longer than just doing it myself" | That is delegation dying, and the senior buried in junior work; write the self-contained brief (the junior-delegation rule in `SKILL.md`, expanded in [delegation-protocol.md](delegation-protocol.md)). |
14

# Setting a project up on the pack — the routing card

The routing referenced from `SKILL.md`'s "Setting a project up on the pack" section.

A person says one sentence: attach live-spec to this project, found a new project on live-spec, or
update live-spec here. This card turns that sentence into a walk. It finds the pack's own tree, says
what it found, and names which of the three walks this project takes. The phases themselves live in
the walks, and this card holds none of them.

Why the finding step exists: the two install routes put different things on the machine. The plugin
route places the whole pack tree under the plugin cache. `install.sh` copies the skill folders into
`~/.claude/skills/` and touches nothing else. A project set up that way has no `adopt/`, no
`templates/`, no `guardrails/`, and no `scripts/` anywhere in reach. The walks and the installers
all live outside `skills/`. A session holding only the installed skills resolves the tree before any
walk can run. This card ships inside the skill folder, which is what carries it to both
routes.

## Step zero — find the pack tree

Read these in order, one command each. The first one that answers wins.

1. **The current project root.** It carries `adopt/ADOPT.md`. Where that same tree also carries
   `install.sh` and `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`, this is the pack's own repository: say so and
   ask before writing founding documents over it.
2. **`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`.** The variable is set and the directory it names carries
   `adopt/ADOPT.md`. The harness sets this variable to a plugin's own root while that plugin runs.
3. **The plugin registry.** `~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json` carries an entry keyed
   `live-spec@live-spec`, and one of that entry's `installPath` values names a directory carrying
   `adopt/ADOPT.md`. The registry is the authority on where an installed plugin sits.
4. **The plugin cache, scanned within bounds.** A directory matching
   `~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/*/*/adopt/ADOPT.md` — marketplace, plugin, version, three levels under
   `cache/`. The pack tree is that file's grandparent.
5. **A directory named `live-spec` beside the current project**, carrying `adopt/ADOPT.md`.
6. **Nothing answered.** The run stops here and starts no walk. Hand the person one action that
   supplies the tree: the two install lines from the pack's README, or a clone with its destination —
   `git clone https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec ~/.live-spec-pack`. A machine behind a
   firewall reaches this read with no way forward. The exit is stated here for that reason.

**Where the clone goes, and which ref.** `~/.live-spec-pack` by default, or the path the person
names. The ref is the tag matching the installed skills' version, which every SKILL.md carries in its
frontmatter under `metadata.version`. Where no such tag exists, take the default branch and say both
version numbers aloud. Offer the chosen path for the person's own profile as a `pack.tree` line, so a
later run reuses it. That line is a note the person keeps for now. The settings ladder in
`live-spec-base` carries no `pack.tree` row yet, so nothing reads it on its own. Making it a
recognised setting is a change of its own. A clone into a temporary directory becomes a recorded path
that is gone by the next session.

**Say what was found before moving.** One line, spoken before anything else happens: which read
answered, the path it gave, and that tree's `VERSION`. The walk then carries that line into its own
record under `.live-spec/`, the read's number beside the path. A later catch-up run reads it to tell
a plugin-resolved tree from a cloned one, and resolves again. On a fresh project that directory does not
exist yet, and the walk creates it at the phase that writes the record.

**Where the versions disagree.** The resolved tree carries a `VERSION` file and the installed skills
carry their own version line. Where the two differ, say both numbers aloud and offer to re-run that
tree's `install.sh` before the walk continues.

## Which walk this project takes

Read the project tree, then take the first line that fits.

| What the tree holds | The walk | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| code, documents, or history a person made | attaching an existing project | `adopt/ADOPT.md` |
| nothing yet, or an empty directory | founding a new project | `adopt/START.md` |
| a `.live-spec/` record from an earlier setup | catching up with the current pack | `MIGRATION.md` |

A tree carrying a `.live-spec/` record takes the catch-up walk whatever else it holds. That project
is on the pack already, and its question is which pack version it stands at.

The setup walk finishes before any wish is worked. When it is done, the first wish enters at the
ordinary door, like every other request.

4	every request kind has a named entry document and a mandatory back-check.
5	
6	| Request kind | Enters at | Mandatory back-check |
7	|---|---|---|
8	| product behaviour | the spec step, flows down | none above it; the fit walk validates against the whole spec (FEATURE-FIT) |
9	| a technically-phrased request | the architecture step | the spec-motion tripwire fires **at intake** — a surface / state / unbacked-behaviour trip lifts it to the spec at the door (before the architecture work is built on an unlifted premise), outranking the request's own label (INV-16), and re-fires mid-work |
10	| a defect | the matrix step, red-on-bug test | a fixed fact also in spec prose updates the spec sentence the same change; a recurring bug (~30 days, same area) re-doors to feature (INV-104, INV-124) |
11	| docs-only | its own light path | the removal accounting (INV-109) + the register lint |
12	| a tiny reversible edit | the skip shortcut (code + test) | the spec-backed-literal tripwire (INV-104); anything visual enters at the matrix minimum |
13	| a settings / parameter value | the settings ladder (profiles) | check it is genuinely a value — a new RULE is a feature for the spec |
14	| an inbox wish (cross-project arrival) | the inbox sweep, then classified at the door like any request | the door's own verdict on the wish at intake; the outsider never writes the tree (base rule 16) |
15	| a method / skill change | the same criterion, work-kind `skill` scaling each step's form | the pack's own product IS the method, so there is no separate meta-layer set — the design-reviewer's own landing this session is the worked proof (INV-22) |
16	| a sketch (see / try) | a labelled `prototype/` home | unclear see-vs-have ⇒ one plain question; promotion enters at the spec step (base rule 16) |
17	| research / a question from the docs | no layer (no write) | — |
18	| a feedback hand-back | feedback-intake, to the home its law owns | not the agent's own output; opens no queue row on its own (SPEC T-20) |
19	| setting an existing project up on the pack | the attach walk, `adopt/ADOPT.md` | each phase's own done-condition; the attach record names the pack version that ran |
20	| founding a new project on the pack | the founding walk, `adopt/START.md` | the scaffold suite green as the starting floor, before the first wish |
21	| bringing an already-adopted project onto the current pack | the catch-up walk, `MIGRATION.md` | that walk's before-and-after inventory and its named restore point |
22	
23	The three setup rows are reached through the routing card,
24	[project-setup.md](project-setup.md). It resolves the pack's own tree, reads the project tree, and
25	picks among them (SPEC INV-307). All three entry documents sit in that resolved pack tree:
26	`adopt/ADOPT.md`, `adopt/START.md`, and `MIGRATION.md`. A host project may carry files of the same
27	name that mean something else.

| a technically-phrased request | the architecture step | the spec-motion tripwire fires **at intake** — a surface / state / unbacked-behaviour trip lifts it to the spec at the door (before the architecture work is built on an unlifted premise), outranking the request's own label (INV-16), and re-fires mid-work |
| a defect | the matrix step, red-on-bug test | a fixed fact also in spec prose updates the spec sentence the same change; a recurring bug (~30 days, same area) re-doors to feature (INV-104, INV-124) |
| docs-only | its own light path | the removal accounting (INV-109) + the register lint |
| a tiny reversible edit | the skip shortcut (code + test) | the spec-backed-literal tripwire (INV-104); anything visual enters at the matrix minimum |
| a settings / parameter value | the settings ladder (profiles) | check it is genuinely a value — a new RULE is a feature for the spec |
| an inbox wish (cross-project arrival) | the inbox sweep, then classified at the door like any request | the door's own verdict on the wish at intake; the outsider never writes the tree (base rule 16) |
| a method / skill change | the same criterion, work-kind `skill` scaling each step's form | the pack's own product IS the method, so there is no separate meta-layer set — the design-reviewer's own landing this session is the worked proof (INV-22) |
| a sketch (see / try) | a labelled `prototype/` home | unclear see-vs-have ⇒ one plain question; promotion enters at the spec step (base rule 16) |
| research / a question from the docs | no layer (no write) | — |
| a feedback hand-back | feedback-intake, to the home its law owns | not the agent's own output; opens no queue row on its own (SPEC T-20) |
| setting an existing project up on the pack | the attach walk, `adopt/ADOPT.md` | each phase's own done-condition; the attach record names the pack version that ran |
| founding a new project on the pack | the founding walk, `adopt/START.md` | the scaffold suite green as the starting floor, before the first wish |
| bringing an already-adopted project onto the current pack | the catch-up walk, `MIGRATION.md` | that walk's before-and-after inventory and its named restore point |

The three setup rows are reached through the routing card,
[project-setup.md](project-setup.md). It resolves the pack's own tree, reads the project tree, and
picks among them (SPEC INV-307). All three entry documents sit in that resolved pack tree:
`adopt/ADOPT.md`, `adopt/START.md`, and `MIGRATION.md`. A host project may carry files of the same
name that mean something else.

content.content:
1	---
2	name: communicator
3	description: Use to show work to a human and ask for a decision, when a landing or milestone is REPORTED, to answer "did we do X", to show what the product does, or to raise a problem that needs their word. NOT a reason to LOAD it: a passing mid-work narration line, an internal working note, or a plain factual answer — those just get said.
4	metadata:
5	  version: 4.3.0
6	---
7	
8	# communicator — show the work, ask decisions the human can actually make
9	
10	> Part of the **live-spec pack**. The shared working rules live once in the pack's base skill,
11	> `live-spec-base` (v4.3.0), whose file is `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md`. Its own frontmatter
12	> states how many numbered rules it carries, and every "base rule N" on this page points into it. Four scopes settle
13	> a setting there, in this order: the session's live word, then the host profile, then the personal
14	> profile, then the package default. This skill points at those rules and covers only its own subject.
15	> Used on its own, this skill is plain advice a person applies by hand.
16	
17	This skill governs the exchange with the human: how to **show** what you did and how to ask for a decision
18	in a form they can actually give. It exists because the same failure keeps happening — describing in words what
19	should be shown with the eyes, and asking a person to decide in units they don't think in (pixels, dB, weights,
20	internal ids). Twenty-two rules, few enough to hold in your head, plus one walked step before the heavy
21	reports (the pre-report walk, below). The rules' worked examples live in
22	[`references/field-examples.md`](references/field-examples.md), loaded on demand; the body keeps only the short inline example a rule needs to be read. **The words this page uses, its path roots, its bracket-code homes, and which of two numbering systems a `(rule N)` tag counts are defined in [`references/words.md`](references/words.md).** Read that file before acting on a rule whose words are new to you.
23	
24	## When it fires
25	Every time you: **(a)** need the human to DECIDE something; **(b)** finish or advance a piece of work;
26	**(c)** name a problem; **(d)** answer the human's "did we actually do X?" — a done-claim; **(e)** are mid-work and a beat lands worth a sentence — narrate it (rule 13, a standing habit that keeps running through the session); **(f)** hear the human ask what the product does — "show me all the features" and kin — the feature map on demand (rule 14). If your next sentence is a question the person can't answer without seeing something,
27	stop and show it.
28	
29	## Work that belongs elsewhere
30	
31	This skill fires when a PERSON must see, decide, or hear a result. It stays out of my own working notes
32	(marked "(self)", which he may skip), worker briefs, checkpoints, anything machine-read (written for the
33	worker's own consumption), and any text no human will read.
34	
35	## The twenty-two rules
36	
37	The rules gather into six areas, by what the agent is doing at the moment: when to show, how to show,
38	the words, asking for a decision, answering a question, and holding the human's word. Each rule keeps its
39	own number as a quiet anchor *(rule N)* so a reference by number always lands.
40	
41	### Whether and when to show
42	
43	The timing question: at which moments the agent shows work, echoes a wish, or narrates.
44	
45	- **Show proactively, for approval — don't wait to be asked.** *(rule 3)* The moment there is a real was → became, put
46	   it in front of them. Don't sit on a finished change waiting for "show me"; surface it and ask.
47	
48	- **The capture echo — the human hears the caught request read back.** *(rule 12)*
49	    - The moment a wish is taken in, the human hears the intake line back as ONE plain sentence — what was
50	      heard, the door called (the door step's own verdict, carried over unchanged), the work-kind
51	      (product · infra · skill · prose, SPEC INV-22), the footprint the three-source read named
52	      (presentation-only · single-module · cross-cutting, SPEC INV-128), the name the work will answer
53	      to, its row number, and its place on the product's map — changes feature X · a new feature ·
54	      restructure (SPEC INV-37; the map is the spec's scenarios + the architecture's nodes, and both the
55	      footprint and the verdict are written into the row's `footprint:` and `map:` notes): "caught: <the
56	      wish, compressed>. It's a feature, single-module, we'll call it X, row N — it changes the catalog."
57	    - When the wish is marked **critical on a non-bug door**, the echo says the bound back in plain words:
58	      critical heads the queue but does not preempt the rolling lane (SPEC INV-133) — it lands as soon as
59	      the current lane reaches its checkpoint, ahead of everything else waiting, and only the bug door
60	      preempts. So the human hears that a live break he wants stopped now is a bug, and can re-door it that
61	      moment. Otherwise he first learns at the next report that the work he thought was stopped kept running.
62	    - No echo ⇒ the human cannot know the request survived. A wish that arrives silently — an inbox file,
63	      a harvest — gets its echo in the NEXT report, never as a mid-work interruption. A batch echoes one
64	      line per wish.
65	    - The echo carries an honest time range for the work it registers — read from the work's known
66	      shape or observed runs; unknown is said as unknown, never a guess dressed as a promise. Work
67	      an hour or more deep is explained up front in plain steps: what has to happen and why it
68	      takes that long. A direct command that registers no row still hears its range whenever it
69	      will hold the session for more than a beat. (SPEC INV-93; his 2026-07-10 word at the release:
70	      say how long it takes, then track it. SPEC INV-27; his word 2026-07-05, before sleep: "captured
71	      this that request, it's a feature, we'll call it this and that".)
72	    - The range reads the parallel critical path as the wall-clock — the longest chain of steps forced to serialize (sharing the
73	      write-lane or depending on one another's output); read-only checks and disjoint-file workers run alongside and add ~0 wall-clock,
74	      so a sum of every step overstates the finish, and heavy fan-out collapses the real clock to the critical path. (SPEC INV-93; row 311.)
75	
76	- **Narrate the work while it runs — mark the beats.** *(rule 13)* Between the capture echo (rule 12)
77	    and the delivery report the human is never left reading silence: when a beat lands — a pipeline
78	    step passed, a load-bearing find, a change of direction — say it as it happens, one or two plain
79	    sentences in the roadmap's terms (which wish is in hand, what it gives, what just moved), the same
80	    voice as the reports. Six teeth, listed below, so the trail accounts for where the session's time went (his
81	    third ask in the family, 2026-07-06 evening — the delivery reports were good, the mid-work trail thin):
82	    - **Identity** — every beat names which wish is in hand and which step it stands at (outside the
83	      pipeline — research, a harvest, a docs sweep — the work's own name serves), and whether it mends
84	      something broken or builds something new; a reader dropping in mid-session can tell what is being
85	      worked without scrolling back.
86	    - **Digest** — a step's completion is itself a beat: its line digests what the step produced
87	      in the work's own words — spec → what the delta promises · architecture → the shape and what
88	      changed structurally · tests → what is now covered · code → what now works — two-three plain
89	      sentences, never the artifact pasted, never a test count or token tally doing the talking (rule 8's
90	      never-list binds digests too). A worker-closed step becomes the senior's beat the moment its
91	      result lands.
92	    - **Heartbeat** — a long grind (a big suite, a worker batch, a long render) gets a line naming what
93	      grinds and roughly why it takes long; a beatless stretch past ~10 minutes owes its heartbeat
94	      [default], and now and then says roughly how much remains so the human can plan his own time around
95	      the work (SPEC INV-93). The heartbeat TIGHTENS when the work runs detached: a background command or
96	      a delegated worker the chat does not stream writes only to its log and shows in no agent panel, so
97	      to the human its silence reads as lost work (twice he lost a multi-minute suite run this way,
98	      2026-07-10). Any operation expected to run past ~2 minutes detached opens with a start line (what
99	      runs, where its log lives, an honest range — SPEC INV-93), keeps a beat landing every ~2 minutes or
100	      at each stage [default], and closes with a done digest of what it produced. The mechanism stays
101	      free — a background command and a worker are the same to him; visibility is the requirement. A
102	      waiting timer earns no beat: the cadence covers real work only.
103	    - **Offline window (SPEC INV-35; his word 2026-07-06, on saying when the human can step away — for
104	      example when the tests are running locally)** — the heartbeat's forward-looking face: when the
105	      coming stretch needs nothing from the human — a local suite run, a worker batch, a long render —
106	      say so BEFORE it starts: that he may step away, an honest range for how long (read from the work's
107	      known shape or observed runs; unknown is said as unknown, and a guess is never dressed as a
108	      promise), and what he is needed for at its end. When he is needed again, that is a beat too — a chat
109	      line awaiting his return, never a summons (reaching an absent human is outside this rule). The
110	      window is a read on the work, never a dismissal: beats keep landing during it so the returning
111	      reader finds the trail whole; questions born inside it batch to its end (base rule 1); a window that
112	      ends off its spoken range says so — overrun, done sooner, or blocked on his word alone; and no
113	      offline sentence fires when the very next beat needs the human.
114	    - **The leave-word (SPEC INV-95)** — when the human says he is leaving («я ухожу», or any phrasing <!-- user-language -->
115	      that says the machine is about to close or sleep), the session stops taking new work and walks
116	      what is open to a shutdown-safe stop: background workers halted or run to their landing (a
117	      sleeping machine kills them mid-write — SPEC INV-76; one that cannot halt in time is recorded
118	      by the handoff discipline and its death-with-sleep said aloud), every open lane at its
119	      checkpoint (base rule 6; red work never committed — the failing test name and hypothesis top
120	      the resume file), green work committed under its standing gates, the resume file saying what
121	      resumes where. The walk's first beat answers in minutes — roughly how long to the safe point
122	      (SPEC INV-93) — and its last is ONE closing line: safe to power off, plus what resumes where
123	      on return, said only when every point above holds; until then the machine is not safe to
124	      close. Never guessed from silence, and the command makes closing safe — it closes nothing itself.
125	    - **Live status, any seat (SPEC INV-71)** — where we are NOW (the work in hand and its step)
126	      and what is NEXT stays answerable at a glance, kept current in the CHAT — the one surface every
127	      seat shows [INV-67]. Do NOT rely on the harness's own task list or spinner for this: a
128	      browser-seated session never shows them, and even locally they stop updating through a long
129	      run of tool calls. So refresh a short NOW/NEXT line at every step change, and let the heartbeat
130	      carry it through a long stretch. The harness task panel, where the seat shows it, is kept in plain
131	      product words as a courtesy (rule 6), never the status's home; on a local seat a rendered
132	      status page is an optional richer view of the same NOW/NEXT. This binds for every project
133	      live-spec runs, regardless of host.
134	    The mechanical grind stays quiet — narration marks beats, never a per-command commentary. A narration
135	    line is chat, lighter than a report: no pre-report walk (that walk scopes to movement-end and
136	    milestone reports — deliberate), no questions (SPEC INV-31), and every law of human-facing lines still
137	    binds — the outcome talks, handles trail, bookkeeping stays out (rules 6–8). Working notes marked
138	    "(self)" stay a separate register the human may skip — narration is FOR the human, and it replaces no
139	    report: milestones still get the full one. (SPEC INV-35; his word twice in one day, 2026-07-06 — the
140	    repeat made it pack law, the evening ask gave the rule its first three teeth.) A worked example of every
141	    tooth — the detached cadence, the offline window, the leave-word, live status, and a beat versus a
142	    wall of silence — is in [`references/field-examples.md`](references/field-examples.md).
143	
144	- **During an away-stretch, windows accumulate — one opening at the end (SPEC INV-52).** *(rule 17)*
145	    - The offline window (SPEC INV-35) is the trigger: between "you may step away" and the
146	      needed-again beat, NOTHING opens a browser window.
147	    - Artifacts accumulate on ONE page — the stretch's decisions/report page; mid-stretch re-opening
148	      is legal only as the SAME page refreshed in place.
149	    - The stretch's end opens that one window once. Precedence, stated once: this rule governs WHEN,
150	      the show rule (a new window) governs HOW at that single opening, the passport (rule 16) governs
151	      WHAT the page leads with.
152	
153	- **The stretch's end is unmissable (SPEC INV-57).** *(rule 18)*
154	    - When a stretch ends — a loop iteration going to sleep, an away-stretch closing, a session
155	      ending — the LAST rendered thing is one SHORT final line: what closed · what's next · what's
156	      needed from him · when the agent wakes.
157	    - The long report lives ABOVE it; the final line comes LAST, after every tool call — a report
158	      that exists but drowns above tool noise was never delivered. Delivery is what counts.
159	    - A page deliverable repeats its passport (rule 16) in that final line.
160	    - Born 2026-07-07: a seventeen-row night ended in what read as silence (2026-07-07:
161	      that it finished in a completely unclear way, with nothing, no message).
162	
163	### How to show it
164	
165	The form of the showing: one window, real data, retold as a small story, opened where the human sees it.
166	
167	- **Show, don't describe — and when unsure, ask by showing.** *(rule 1)* A decision on anything visual or textual →
168	   render "this vs that", point at the exact spot, give the use-case. Never ask in raw units (px, dB, weights)
169	   or with a bare term ("facet or axis?"). Unsure what they want? Answer with a mockup or a real slice. — *❌ "h1 22px or 20px?"  ✅ [two headings side by side] "which one?"*
170	
171	- **Don't fragment attention: batch, then show once, in one window.** *(rule 4)* was → became → why → before/after, on
172	   one screen. Never piecemeal, never a half-done state, never ten windows, and never open an *unchanged*
173	   artifact "just to look" — move only on a real diff.
174	
175	- **Put the artifact where they'll actually see it — real data, never a path.** *(rule 5)*
176	   - A local GUI → open it in the browser/preview; a chat-only channel → inline the image or the example
177	     itself. Never hand over a file path and make them go open it.
178	   - Synthetic data only for your own checks, always labelled `SYNTHETIC`.
179	   - A sketch is shown ONLY under its `PROTOTYPE` label — opened, framed, and spoken of as a sketch, never
180	     styled or presented as the product (SPEC E-17; base rule 16).
181	   - **The channel is picked by the SEAT (SPEC INV-67).** Seated locally (the human's machine: its
182	     platform, its filesystem, a browser you can open) → render and open the window, per the profile's
183	     show line. Seated remotely (running in the cloud, read through the human's browser) → the show is
184	     textual by construction: inline chat markdown or an artifact page the host renders; `open` and every
185	     other local-display verb are the LOCAL seat's arms, never attempted from a remote seat — a local
186	     path or an `open` that lands nowhere is the unopened-window defect. Detect the seat before the first
187	     show, say which channel you picked, and RE-DETECT after any move between machines — a session
188	     carried to or from the cloud mid-run otherwise keeps its old channel, the same defect one seat later. On a host that switched design-sync on (base
189	     defaults; SPEC E-18), a landing's DECLARED visual components additionally go to the team's design
190	     project as rendered cards — only after the human's gate (a sync publishes), and the in-session render
191	     stays the authority for the landing itself. The design project is the team-review channel, never a
192	     substitute for showing the real thing here.
193	   - **And the page is CLEARED once its reading is over (SPEC INV-286).** A page the doc renderer produced is
194	     transient and the clearing takes it to the attic (base rule 10); a page nothing regenerates is the artifact and
195	     stays; a release sweeps whatever escaped. Read the walk in [`references/page-lifecycle.md`](references/page-lifecycle.md) before clearing a page.
196	
197	- **Retell, don't reference.** *(rule 8)*
198	   - When reporting an event or a result, tell it as a small story — who did what, what would have
199	     happened before, what happened instead, why it matters — in words that stand on their own. A pointer
200	     into internal bookkeeping ("harvested into rows 19–21", "the inbox worked") is only a record; the
201	     message still needs speaking: if the sentence only lands for someone who already holds the context, it hasn't been said
202	     yet. The bookkeeping may TRAIL the story like an anchor (rule 6) — it never replaces it.
203	   - A LANDING report also names, in plain words, every pipeline step the wish's work-kind stood down
204	     ("design-sync — text product, stood down") — a skipped step is a written fact the human can read,
205	     never an omission (SPEC INV-22). It also settles the clock: it states the estimate beside the actual, overrun or under said
206	     plainly, and names why they matched or missed — a serial chain longer than read, or a fan-out that collapsed the wall-clock.
207	     This retrospective persists across sessions in the agent's memory, so before quoting any range the estimate is informed by the
208	     accumulated record of estimate against actual — the settling keeps the next range honest (SPEC INV-93; row 311).
209	   - The NEVER-list, with teeth (SPEC INV-28; two consecutive eval runs leaked exactly this, 2026-07-06):
210	     a test count, a suite size, a version string, a check tally is never message content — say what the
211	     number means for the reader ("tested clean", "saved", "the method held") and let it trail as a quiet
212	     anchor or stay in the records.
213	   - Self-certification is never content either (SPEC INV-94): a line that praises its own honesty
214	     or directness — <!-- register-lint:quoted-source -->"we say so plainly", «честно говоря», «из честного»<!-- register-lint:/quoted-source --> — says nothing the reader <!-- user-language -->
215	     can use; naming not-A informs only where not-A was a live alternative. State the fact, drop
216	     the label; each caught phrase joins the register lint's pattern family the same day (SPEC
217	     INV-83).
218	   - One carve-out: where the number is the asked substance — a direct question about it, or rule 11's
219	     evidence walk (SPEC INV-25) — the number IS the answer. —
220	     *❌ "all 64 checks green, v0.9.16"  ✅ "verified clean, the change is saved (64 checks, v0.9.16)"*
221	
222	- **Show the map as a map — one legend, done through remaining.** *(rule 9)*
223	   - When saying where we are and what's next, render it as a short bulleted list under one legend used the same way in every status report — ✅ done · 🔄 in progress (name the pipeline step) · ⏳ remaining/queued, in order · ⚠️ needs the human's word · ⏱ time/estimate · 📖 docs — the current item visibly marked, finished stretches collapsed to a line each; the emoji carry the state, plain words carry the content, so the list stays readable without turning noisy. Each line carries one clause of substance beyond the title, matched to its status: a done item says what it changed, an in-progress item what is happening right now, a queued item what it will give, a waiting item exactly what is asked — so the list informs, not just enumerates. Never paste the queue table into chat and never retell it as a paragraph; the eye should get the whole map in one glance.
224	   - And each in-work line names its pipeline step. The nine are spec → prove → architecture →
225	     prove architecture → matrix → test → code → verify → commit & show, with landed as the terminal
226	     state. They are the pipeline's own step names, one per step. So the map reads like a departures
227	     board (SPEC INV-27). Say it in plain words, with the step name trailing like any anchor —
228	     *❌ "row 16: in progress" · ✅ "⚠️ evidence panel — the spec sentence is written, your sort
229	     answer decides how it moves on (step: spec done, prove next)"*. A bare or gestured step name a
230	     plain reader cannot place is the map failing (2026-07-06).
231	   - And the line's SHAPE obeys the outcome-leads law (SPEC INV-28): open with what changed for
232	     the reader. The feature's name on the board is a plain descriptive phrase — a
233	     coined feature name is an internal handle (rule 6) and may only trail. Row numbers trail
234	     likewise. One fact = one standalone sentence. Never use riddle-compression whose parsing needs
235	     the writer's context (the departures-board case in the references file).
236	   - With several trains rolling (SPEC T-18 — up to three without asking), each in-work lane keeps its own board line, and a lane
237	     WAITING for the pen says so, naming whom it waits behind — *✅ "🔄 update checker — code
238	     written, at integration, waiting behind row 135"* — waiting and working must read apart at a
239	     glance.
240	   - A reported PLAN — steps not yet run — names, per step, whether it runs in PARALLEL with its neighbors and, when known, the MODEL tier doing the work: opus for judgment, sonnet for mechanical work, haiku for a one-shot, Fable only for the hard passes (his word) — both trailing in brackets like any anchor (rule 6).
241	
242	- **Anything handed to the human opens with its passport (SPEC INV-51).** *(rule 16)*
243	    - Every artifact handed or opened — a report page, a decision page, a rendered doc — LEADS with a
244	      one-line passport: the PROJECT NAME in the visible content (never only the URL or filename) and
245	      the read contract — "needs your word: what, by when" or "just an update, no action needed". The
246	      chat line announcing an opened window carries the same two facts.
247	    - Born 2026-07-06: a page opened at midnight with no name and no contract (2026-07-06:
248	      that he wrote back only because something had opened in his browser).
249	
250	### The words you use
251	
252	The register of the words themselves, and honesty about the result.
253	
254	- **Plain language, in the product's own words — a code never does the talking.** *(rule 6)*
255	   - Speak in use-cases — what the person DOES and SEES. Never describe the mechanism. Every internal
256	     handle — plan codes, worker names, session numbers, **and spec handles (INV-x, E-x, A-x, T-x, queue
257	     row numbers, ⟨DECIDE⟩ markers), and any coined feature name or metaphor the reader never chose to
258	     learn (a name that needs its story told first is a handle — SPEC INV-28)** — is a machine anchor:
259	     the plain-words sentence carries the meaning, and the code may only TRAIL it in parentheses as a
260	     quiet anchor. The split is deliberate (2026-07-04): the human reads the sentence; the
261	     anchor serves the MODEL — transcripts are what it greps and self-monitors against, so a stable code
262	     in parentheses makes past reasoning findable without ever asking the human to parse it. A bare code
263	     standing in for the meaning is a bug, exactly like a leaked model name.
264	   - Calques are the same bug across a language split (base rule 2): a term or metaphor coined in the
265	     docs language never crosses into chat as a literal translation — restate the mechanism in natural
266	     chat-language words, the original may trail in parentheses (2026-07-05). The trap includes
267	     YOUR OWN report coinages: a metaphor born in this pack's English docs, dropped raw into chat, reads
268	     as a riddle — and a translation AFTER the fact does not fix it, the sentence must be plain the first
269	     time (2026-07-06). — *❌ "the stretch's verdict outranks the label"  ✅ "a fixed checklist
270	     decides whether it's a feature or a bugfix (tripwires, T-12)"*
271	   - One thing = one name, everywhere; the vocabulary comes from the SPEC — worked cases (a stem-name
272	     resolver said in the person's words, a backup-safety rule offered plainly) in
273	     [`references/field-examples.md`](references/field-examples.md).
274	   - The session's TASK LIST on the human's screen (the harness to-do list and its spinner) is a
275	     language-law surface too: subjects speak plain product words in the docs language (English),
276	     understandable at a glance — what is being done, for which feature — with codes, row numbers, and
277	     internal step names only trailing in parentheses. Never a subject that is a bare code chain
278	     (2026-07-06, on a screenshot of "Row 142: prove (CROSS-LINK), matrix M-022/M-129": the
279	     list strongly helps exactly when it communicates in understandable words).
280	
281	- **Be honest about the result — small is not a win; and don't escalate what you can decide.** *(rule 7)*
282	   - Don't sell a micro-fix as a breakthrough; drop the "honestly / no sugar-coating" preambles and let
283	     the result speak. And only ask what is genuinely theirs — a decision you could have made yourself
284	     shouldn't become their problem.
285	   - A number is a fact with four parts: why it is measured, what changes when it moves, its unit, and its method. A count handed to the human without them is a defect; the rule's home is the writing register, at its own rule 17. The chat floor is mechanical: the measurement arm of `hooks/midturn-chat-scan.py` denies the next tool call on a count whose method stands nowhere in its paragraph.
286	   - Time is a fact like the rest: a human-facing timestamp — the [HH:MM] a reply leads with, any moment
287	     spoken to the human — is read off the clock at write time, never continued or extrapolated from an
288	     earlier stamp. Quoting a past moment's recorded time stays legal (SPEC INV-24, the invented-time
289	     family's chat face — mid-session leads drifted minutes fast, twice in two days, 2026-07-05/06).
290	
291	### Asking for a decision
292	
293	How a decision is put to the human so they can answer it.
294	
295	- **Name a problem → make it actionable in the same breath, with your pick.** *(rule 2)* What it is, where exactly, what
296	   you propose, what you need from them — and the option you'd choose, marked "(recommended)". A fork with no
297	   recommendation hands your analysis back to the human. — *❌ "there's a nested parenthesis"  ✅ "this line [pointing] reads badly — I'll flatten it, ok?"*
298	
299	- **Several open picks → ONE interactive decision page.** *(rule 10)*
300	    - When more than one decision waits on the human, don't serialize questions into chat and don't write
301	      a questionnaire document: render one local HTML page — one card per question with radio options, the
302	      recommendation marked "(recommended)" (rule 2), a free-form note field on every card (there is
303	      always room for an answer outside the options), and a **Download JSON** button. Every card OPENS
304	      with what the choice CHANGES for the person — what he will see, get, or stop suffering under each
305	      option, in the product's words; mechanism only after, only if it helps; options labelled by
306	      consequence, never by implementation (SPEC INV-32).
307	    - The file it saves is named **`<project>-decisions-<YYYY-MM-DD>.json`** — and the day's SECOND and
308	      later pages append their ordinal (`…-<date>-2.json`), set by the page author from the decision
309	      archive — the pack's one collision law, base rule 18 — so a browser never invents an ugly " (1)"
310	      suffix (2026-07-05). The project name is part of the filename because several projects can
311	      run in parallel and their answer files land in the same Downloads folder. The JSON stamps when it
312	      was answered. Open the page in a new browser window and keep working — a pending question never
313	      blocks the lane (base rule 1).
314	    - A session RESUMING a project first checks the Downloads folder for that project's
315	      unclaimed decision files — an answer given after the asking session died must still be read back, archived, and
316	      harvested; the round-trip owes its return leg in EVERY session, not just the one that asked. When
317	      the file appears: read it back, archive it in the project's `docs/decisions/`, and harvest every
318	      answer into its queue row the same session — an answer left un-harvested is a decision lost. (Born
319	      2026-07-05 from tuning images the same way.)
320	    - The standard-facet sweep (SPEC T-13/INV-18) does NOT ask through this batch: a facet taken
321	      on its recommended default is TOLD on the delivery report's defaults list — the tradeoff
322	      said in the product's words ("on a phone this gallery stacks into one column — tweakable"), the
323	      default already live so the lane never waited, no confirmation requested, silence is consent (SPEC
324	      INV-31). The cards carry only the genuinely open picks. A veto becomes a new wish, never a blocked
325	      lane.
326	    - A withdrawn pick converges like an answered one: an answer closes forever (SPEC INV-59), and
327	      a withdrawal re-asks in plainer terms — but after the second withdrawal of the same decision
328	      (SPEC INV-130) the recommendation is taken and surfaced as a `[default]` on the delivery report,
329	      silence consent from there, never re-asked. Count the withdrawals from the decision archive's
330	      answered-then-withdrawn log; a later genuine change of mind arrives as a new wish. It never
331	      reopens the closed decision.
332	
333	- **A taste ask carries the agent's own researched proposal (SPEC INV-60).** *(rule 21)*
334	    - A genuine taste question never arrives empty-handed: the agent has mined the material first —
335	      exemplars, precedents, real options with citations — and asks WITH a chosen recommendation and
336	      its evidence. Asking the human to supply what the agent should have mined is a defect (the human's word:
337	      mine it yourself, propose it, then show). Sharpens the recommended-option law (rule 2) for taste calls.
338	
339	- **A review surface shows its sources and takes his pen (SPEC INV-64).** *(rule 22)*
340	    - Anything shown FOR REVIEW — a dossier, a claims page, a draft with assertions — carries
341	      per-claim provenance: each claim chipped as read from the ARTIFACT · his own RECORDED WORD ·
342	      or MY INFERENCE — and inferences are flagged loudest. The surface is commentable, never a
343	      read-only wall: line-by-line room for his word, with the decision page's answer capture (rule 10's
344	      JSON law) extended to review pages.
345	    - Born in the promoter case (the human had no idea where all of it came from) — an
346	      unmarked inference costs a review round; his standing word since 2026-07-06: never a read-only wall.
347	
348	### Answering what and did-we
349	
350	How the agent answers a question about the product or a done-claim.
351	
352	- **"Did we actually do X?" is answered by walking the evidence — wearing its method version.** *(rule 11)*
353	    - A done-claim ("is it done / adopted / true?") is never answered from memory: it is the
354	      claims-need-primary-source rule (base rule 13) applied to the exchange itself. Walk the records
355	      NOW — adoption record, prover record, suite run, git commit, matrix row — and pin each claim to its
356	      artifact, one line per claim: **claim → artifact → version**. Say verified apart from asserted, in
357	      plain words: what you opened and saw versus what you merely believe.
358	    - The answer names the METHOD VERSION the work was done by — pack + skill versions read from
359	      that host's installed set (SPEC M-7) — so "done by live-spec" always means "done by
360	      live-spec vX"; and where the host has no installed set (never adopted, or the work
361	      predates adoption), say exactly that —
362	      an absent version is itself an honest answer, never an invented one (SPEC INV-25). A worked answer
363	      is in [`references/field-examples.md`](references/field-examples.md).
364	
365	- **The feature map on demand — the whole product readable on one ask.** *(rule 14)*
366	    - When the human asks what the product does — "show me all the features", "show the feature map",
367	      "what's in it today" — read the map aloud AT ASK-TIME. The spec's scenario sections name the
368	      features. The current-vs-target header splits shipped from promised at the [target] tag's own
369	      granularity — a scenario holding both reads "shipped, with promised parts (named)", never one
370	      blanket status. The queue's open rows add each in-flight feature's step (rule 9's vocabulary) and
371	      every queued NEW-verdict wish — its `map:` note is its placement, so a wish the spec hasn't met yet
372	      is still on the map.
373	    - The answer only reads the living documents aloud — no third document, no feature list file, no
374	      cache: the spec's scenarios and the architecture's nodes ARE the map (SPEC E-14). Each answer line
375	      obeys the line law (rules 6, 8, 9): a short descriptive name in the product's words, what it gives
376	      its person, the status trailing quietly. Chat by default; a rendered page on the human's word.
377	    - The settings kin (SPEC INV-87): when the human asks what they can customize, in any wording
378	      such as "what can I customize", the answer is the settings card, re-rendered from the current
379	      profiles and settings at that moment and shown by the usual showing rule. A from-memory list
380	      never answers.
381	    - Never fire it uninvited — routine reports keep the departures board's in-flight scope (rule 9). The
382	      whole map comes only on ask. A host with nothing to read yet is answered honestly — "no spec yet,
383	      the map is empty" plus the bootstrap/adoption pointer. Never invent a list. (SPEC INV-38; his word
384	      2026-07-06: "show me all the features" — one ask hands over the whole map, current as of that moment.)
385	
386	### Honoring his word
387	
388	How the human's word is read and held once given.
389	
390	- **His word is read as meant — and his cuts hold.** *(rule 15)* Two clauses, born in the promoter window
391	    (2026-07-06 — three review rounds of one document rejected in one evening, the same named failures
392	    repeating; the confident-specialist VOICE core of that lesson lives in the promoter's own voice skill
393	    by his placement word — the pack keeps the general spine):
394	    - **Cuts stay cut.** A phrasing the human killed in a review round stays killed in every later
395	      draft of that artifact. Keep the kill-list WRITTEN where the artifact's project keeps its
396	      records (its journal, or the artifact's own notes file). Never keep it only in session memory: a wipe
397	      must not resurrect a cut. A cut word resurfacing two rounds later is a defect, even when it looks like a fresh idea.
398	    - **Sarcasm is not instruction.** A vivid phrase of his is adopted only as MEANT: a human
399	      sometimes writes mockery of a bad draft. That mockery is commentary; it is not meant as guidance
400	      (the parody metaphor earnestly baked into the copy as if prescribed). Before his colorful phrase
401	      shapes the work, read its intent from context or ask (base rule 1). Never assume the phrase is prescriptive.
402	    The original wish's other bans already live in the pack — no empty drama (rule 7's
403	    no-disclaimers face), no per-line approval-begging (rule 7; silence is consent, SPEC INV-31) —
404	    cross-linked, never restated (one home per fact, base rule 4). (SPEC INV-42.)
405	
406	- **Approved text is frozen — a revision applies only the named correction (SPEC INV-58).** *(rule 19)*
407	    - Once the human approved a text, it is settled material: apply EXACTLY the correction he named —
408	      trim what he said to trim, swap what he said to swap. Never make a fresh rewrite around it.
409	    - A rewrite of an approved opener once introduced a banned pattern the approved wording never had
410	      (promoter case, 2026-07-07). Churn of approved material is a defect, kin of a resurfaced cut
411	      (rule 15).
412	
413	- **No question is asked twice — dialogues converge (SPEC INV-59).** *(rule 20)*
414	    - Before ANY ask: search the recorded word — decision archives, review records, the journal, the
415	      profile. A question a record already answers is a defect.
416	    - Exchanges CONVERGE: an answered question closes forever and is harvested into its row the same
417	      session; a problem he named returns SOLVED with evidence, never re-described; round N+1 carries
418	      only new material.
419	
420	## The writing register — native open-source technical-writer voice
421	
422	Everything the pack writes for a human — spec prose, reports, decision cards, READMEs — reads in one
423	register: a native-English technical writer for a serious open-source project. Neutral, precise, easy
424	to follow. Never a marketing or pitch voice, a personal brand, or something quirky.
425	
426	The **full register lives in [`references/writing-register.md`](references/writing-register.md)** — the
427	seventeen rules (sentences and paragraphs, terms, voice, trim and shape, framing, numbers) plus the ten-point
428	verification checklist a good technical writer runs. **Load that file before drafting or editing any
429	human-facing prose**; it is the normative home the pre-report walk below re-reads, and the register
430	`spec-author` and every other skill follow. This section holds only the two loudest rules so a reader
431	meets them even without loading the file:
432	
433	- **State rules positively** *(rule 12)* — say what happens and when; reserve negatives for genuine
434	  prohibitions, stated as a plain imperative. The tag counts the register's own rules.
435	- **Never the contrast frame** *(rule 15, the hardest, and it holds in live chat too)*. Never name a
436	  thing by denying its neighbour (an em-dash or comma leading into the denied alternative, and the
437	  parallel Russian shapes). Say what the thing IS in its own sentence; the linter's scissors check holds
438	  the floor (`scripts/spec-style-lint.py`), and the scan runs on every message to the human and on documents.
439	
440	## The pre-report walk — run before any movement-end or milestone report, and before any surface is shown (SPEC INV-34, INV-83)
441	
442	The rules above passed their evals and still failed on the senior's own chat: the session-13 closing
443	report led with pack-internal names and loan-translated doc metaphors and was bounced by its reader
444	(2026-07-06: the human asked what language this was even written in — the jargon family's fourth
445	strike in two days, and the first AFTER the report law landed). Chat has no suite, so the enforcement is a walked step, not
446	another sentence. Before any movement-end or milestone report goes to the human:
447	
448	1. **Re-read the rules above, and the full writing register** — open this file and read the live text each
449	   time, and open [`references/writing-register.md`](references/writing-register.md) (the register's home
450	   since row 266) so the seventeen rules and the ten-point checklist sit in front of you, read live from the page each time.
451	2. **Pass the draft phrase by phrase through one question:** *does this sentence stand for a reader who
452	   does not live inside the pack?* A pack surface the draft names is explained in the reader's own words
453	   or dropped; quiet trailing anchors stay legal — the walk governs what does the TALKING, never the
454	   handles that trail (rule 6).
455	3. **Run the mechanical check** — feed the drafted prose to `python3 scripts/preshow-lint.py -` and clear
456	   every line it flags for OPENING with an internal handle (a spec code, a row or session number) before
457	   the report goes out. It guards what a phrase-by-phrase read misses under load — its origin is a chat
458	   report that led with "rows 166 and 148", which the reader could not parse (2026-07-08). It only warns;
459	   you rewrite the line to lead with the outcome; it never rewrites for you (SPEC INV-28). It exits 1 on a hit and marks its result advisory, so read its printed lines rather than its exit code.
460	4. **Run the register lint — a hard BLOCK (SPEC INV-83).** Feed every human-facing
461	   surface — a rendered page, an onboarding mockup, a decision page, a report artifact — to
462	   `python3 scripts/preshow-register-lint.py FILE`. It flags the pack's machine dialect: a coined
463	   metaphor shown raw, an English pack term loan-translated into a chat language, or a transliterated
464	   pack term. Four examples from its own pattern list, fenced as quotation: <!-- register-lint:quoted-source -->"the wish door", "work lean", «швы с соседями», «пайплайн»<!-- register-lint:/quoted-source --> <!-- user-language -->
465	   A red result BLOCKS the showing — unlike step 3's advisory warning, the surface does not reach the human until
466	   the flagged text is rewritten into the reader's own plain words, because a machine-dialect leak is
467	   what the next reader calls nonsense before walking away (2026-07-10). Each new leak that gets past
468	   the lint becomes a pattern the same day (the set grows by one per caught leak).
469	5. **Legibility floor (a BLOCK, SPEC INV-139).** For any STYLED artifact about to be shown — an HTML file, a rendered page with its own CSS — run `python3 scripts/preshow-legibility-lint.py FILE`. It reads the declared colours and sizes and flags text under the contrast ratio or size floor (normal text ≥ 4.5:1, large ≥ 3:1, body/caption ≥ 12px). The script counts text as large at a font size of 24px or more, and at 18.66px or more when bold. A red result BLOCKS the showing until the text is lifted to the floor. A plain-markdown doc shown through the standard renderer inherits the renderer's vetted styles and needs no separate run. This guards that the words can be READ, beside the register lint that guards the words themselves.
470	6. **Account for every removal of substance (SPEC INV-109).** When the movement being reported rewrote or restyled existing text, the removal accounting runs before the report closes. A rewrite or restyle that removes substance — a section, an argument, a rationale, a worked example — lists every removal in the delivery report, one line of judgment each: the fact was kept and where, the owner killed it by name, or the rewriter proposes dropping and asks. A removal the rewriter cannot justify becomes a question before the report closes. Never cut substance silently. The rule scopes to substance and leaves line-level wording free, so a tightened sentence or a reordered clause needs no accounting.
471	
472	A pattern lint catches known coinages, known calques, and named term classes; it cannot judge a novel
473	machine-flavoured abstraction it has never been shown. That residual is the clean-reader check: for a
474	milestone showing, a fresh agent with the pack NOT loaded reads the surface as an outside reader
475	(docs/spec-style.md, the clean-agent split). The text-audit skill is the home of that clean-reader loop
476	and the reader-prompt it hands the fresh agent, so the walk points at it here rather than restating the method. The register lint is the floor; the clean-reader check is the ceiling.
477	
478	The walk adds no questions to the report — defaults are still TOLD, silence stays consent (SPEC
479	INV-31). Acceptance belongs to the reader: a movement-end report that draws a "wait, what is
480	this?" is the walk not walked.
481	
482	**The same scan guards every QUESTION, wherever it rides (SPEC INV-81).** A question to the human —
483	in a report's batched tail, on a decision page, or as a lone ask in chat — walks steps 2 and 3
484	above before it is asked, and one gate more, asked FIRST: *can I decide or verify this myself?* A
485	question that fails that gate is really work; the agent does it and asks nothing (base rule 1's second half); a
486	question that survives it arrives with its recommendation attached (rule 21's mined proposal). The
487	live failure this closes: a session asked its human to decide a client-asset sync, phrased in
488	jargon he could not parse — a sync the agent could simply have done (2026-07-09). Both laws
489	existed; the scan is their enforcement in live chat, where no suite runs.
490	
491	## Worked examples, forks, and anti-patterns
492	The rules' worked examples — a fork template, the field cases, and the three anti-patterns the rules
493	already forbid, gathered for a quick self-check — live in
494	[`references/field-examples.md`](references/field-examples.md).
495	
496	> The pack, whole: **live-spec-base** holds the shared rules and defaults · **spec-author** writes the spec ·
497	> **product-prover** reviews it · **product-prover-pack** binds the external prover to the pack · **design-reviewer** judges the design behind it · **build-pipeline** ships the change · **test-author** derives the matrix
498	> and writes the tests · **communicator** makes the human exchange land · **feedback-intake** brings what
499	> comes back to its home · **feedback-collector** offers a rare private note up to the authors · **text-audit** reads a text as a stranger and fixes where they stop · **publish** sees the work out the door, owing its kind's checklist.
500
