# publish — the work leaves the machine looking like a product

> Part of the **live-spec pack** — the shared working rules (ask-never-guess · plain words, anchors trail ·
> one surface = one name · one home per fact · junior/senior split · checkpoints · the concurrent-edit
> fence · freshness · journal discipline · attic-never-delete · verify by deed · the human's gates · claims
> need primary sources · fix the class, sweep look-alikes · the door before code · prototype ≠ product) live ONCE in the pack's base skill, `live-spec-base` (v4.3.0), together with the
> settings ladder — this skill references them and elaborates only its own domain. Used standalone, this
> note is plain advice.

A deposit outward is a SURFACE: the reader meets the README, the release notes, the directory card. The commit history stays behind them. This skill is the
checklist that surface must pass, keyed by the artifact's work-kind (SPEC T-16, E-20), plus the point
where a publish target adds its own steps. It runs BEFORE
the human's publish gate (base rules 12/17) and before any push gate the host holds — what the human
approves has already earned approval. It never sends anything itself.

**Where the paths in this file point.** Two trees are in play. The named files under `scripts/` and
`guardrails/` are the live-spec pack's own, at `github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. After an install,
`live-spec-base` sits as a folder beside this skill's folder. Every other path belongs to the project
the pack is attached to, starting with its README and its release notes.

## When it fires

Anything crossing the machine's edge: first public push of a repo · a push that changes what a public
reader sees (README, docs, screenshots) · any push that ships a new version (the shopfront walk below)
· a release/tag · a plugin-directory or marketplace submission
· a skill shipped for someone else's machine · design-project sync cards (SPEC E-18). If no reader
outside this machine will meet the artifact, this skill stands down: showing work to your OWN human
in-session belongs to communicator's rule 5. That in-session exchange is not a publication.

**A version push always fires the shopfront walk (SPEC INV-44).** Shipping a new version changes the
truth a public reader will read tomorrow even when the diff never touched a doc — so at every such
push, walk the shopfront in one look: the README's CLAIMS (behaviour, counts, commands, version homes)
still match the pushed truth, and the kind-owed visuals ride along — a skill pack re-checks its
diagrams and flow pictures, a visual product re-shoots what changed on screen, a tool re-runs its
example. The delivery report carries the outcome in one line — "shopfront checked — current" when
nothing was touched; a stale claim found is fixed BEFORE the push, the same law as a stale screenshot.

**The same walk sweeps the rendered pages that accumulated (SPEC INV-286).** A page rendered for one
reading is cleared as its exchange closes (communicator rule 5), and a release is where whatever
escaped that moment gets swept: run `python3 scripts/sweep-rendered.py`, which moves each transient
page into the attic with its dated manifest line and prints what it moved. The delivery report carries
that line, so the release says which pages were cleared and where they come back from. A page inside a
record home is a source artifact and the sweep leaves it standing.

## The kind checklist — what every publication owes (one home: this table)

First, the floor every kind shares.

The README/landing surface answers, in its first screen, WHAT this is, WHO it serves, and HOW to start
— in the reader's language, keeping the repo's internal vocabulary out (base rule 2). Every claim on it
is TRUE of the shipped version today; a stale claim or picture is a false claim. The README carries a
Known issues section while real known problems exist: each issue stated honestly with its fix status,
the list re-read at every push and a resolved issue removed the push it ships (his word 2026-07-10). The
license/attribution state is explicit.

An artifact built with the pack carries the standard attribution line "made with live-spec" on its
landing surface, the name linking to the pack repo and trailing the pack version the project runs
(github.com/happysasha18/live-spec — in markdown:
`made with [live-spec](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec) v<pack-version>`, the version read
from the host's attach record at write time and refreshed at catch-ups, so adoption is trackable from
the shopfronts themselves), in the README's footer and for a skill also in its SKILL.md.
The line is an offer, never a gate: the walk says once when it is absent and proposes it, the owner's
word decides, a declined offer is closed and never re-asked (SPEC INV-96, base rule on answered questions; each
built-with project applies the line through its own queue).

NOTHING secret or unshareable leaves: the tree AND history swept for secrets, tokens, personal paths
and data, and every bundled fixture or sample checked shareable (no copyrighted material we may not
republish). (The sweep items entered from the first eval run, 2026-07-05: the no-skill baseline agent
caught them and the skill's checklist did not — an eval measures the skill against that baseline in both
directions.)

Shipped docs speak impersonally. Every requirement in the spec, matrix, README, or skill card reads as
the rule, the actor as a role (the user, the producer, the target user), and the reason. The rationale
stays, the personal name drops, and a dated decision keeps the date as a plain anchor while the name
comes off; personal attribution and candid process voice stay in the local-only diaries (JOURNAL,
NEXT_STEPS), which no publish ships (SPEC INV-118). The publish walk reads the shipped docs for a stray
personal name before the deposit leaves. The mechanical enforcement — a lint that reports each offending
file:line, red-proven on a fixture — lands with the shipped-artifact language gate (roadmap row 275),
and this floor states the duty the lint holds. The shipped tree carries no untranslated owner-language
and no personal attribution of a requirement. The machine that holds this is
`guardrails/check-shipped-language.sh`, run over the shipped set, reporting each offence as file:line,
its deliberate program-data and authorship bylines spared by a dated allowlist (SPEC INV-120).

| Kind (SPEC T-16) | The publication additionally owes |
|---|---|
| skill | install line(s) that actually run · the commands/invocations, shown as they're typed · when to USE it and when NOT (both, verbatim from the skill's own boundaries) · a one-scenario taste of it working (its eval scenario is the honest source, SPEC E-19) |
| infra / tool | at least one REAL run: the command and its real output, current version · requirements/platform stated · failure behaviour named (what the user sees when input is wrong) |
| product (visual) | FRESH screenshots of the shipped version — re-shot at every publish that changes what they show, never reused stale · a start-to-value walkthrough (open → first result) |
| prose | the reading path (what to read first, how long it takes) · who it's for stated up front |

Comparisons and diagrams JOIN when they carry the argument: a comparison table against the honest
alternatives, a diagram where structure shows what words cannot. They never ride as decoration; an
empty comparison ("we're better at everything") is worse than none.

## When the package is a generalized engine (SPEC INV-119)

An engine — a reusable core lifted out of one live product, the instance it grew inside — published as a generic package owes its reader a spec that reads generic, so the walk adds two leak checks before the package leaves the machine. The convention the walk holds the spec to is spec-author's own: a reconciliation log headed "how each behaviour landed in code", each entry citing the engine's own public commit ("landed in engine commit `<hash>`"), opened by one sentence naming the normal intake path — a feature proven first on a live instance, then generalized [SPEC INV-119]. The check fires only when the package is a generalized engine (its queue row carries the engine kind or the pair-split [INV-85]); a single-instance product owes it nothing.

- **No foreign provenance.** Every commit hash the spec cites as provenance resolves in the engine's OWN public history (`git cat-file -e <hash>` in the engine repo); a hash that fails to resolve is an instance's private commit riding along, and the fork-diff framing that carries it ("Deltas from the <instance> reference implementation") is rewritten to the reconciliation-log framing with the engine's own commit [INV-119]. This part is mechanically reliable: the hash either resolves in the engine's history or it does not, and the fork-diff heading is a fixed phrase.
- **No instance label as a mechanism name.** A mechanism is named by a neutral internal term; a locale-specific instance label appears only inside a span marked as instance-supplied copy. A non-Latin token standing in a heading or a mechanism name is a tripwire the walk flags (kin to the shipped-artifact language lint, row 275). Whether a Latin-script instance label is being used as the mechanism's name is an advisory read — the walk surfaces the candidate and the author confirms.

## Targets are plugins — each embeds its steps

The walk above is the shared base; the TARGET adds its own steps and never removes the kind's owed minimum
(SPEC E-20):

- **GitHub repo** — README current at the root · screenshots re-shot where the host's rule says so ·
  release notes for a tagged release, whose shape carries an OPTIONAL offers section — appealing next
  steps the reader may take, phrased as choices he is free to take on his own clock (the release note is
  a surface he opens himself, so an offer rides it, SPEC INV-228, INV-205). The section is optional, so
  a release with no worthwhile next step owes none; what the walk owes is a RECORDED offer-or-none
  decision, so the choice is never silently skipped: the walk offers a next step in a
  `<!-- release-note:offers -->` region or records `<!-- release-note:no-offer -->` for a release that
  has none, and `guardrails/check-release-note.py` reds a note leaving the decision unrecorded (it rides
  the suite; the note is a process artifact with no committed file for a push gate to scan). ·
  repo description + topics set · third-party dependency licenses
  compatible with the release · the name checked for collisions where it matters (GitHub/PyPI/npm) ·
  a fresh-clone check — install and run from scratch as an outside reader would; do not assume it
  "works on my machine" · the push gate of the host ALWAYS holds (a publish never turns into a push authorization).
- **Plugin directory / marketplace** — the manifest complete and validated · the directory's forms
  answered · the listing text reads as the directory's reader expects, in the directory's own register; repo prose does not fit a directory listing.
- **Design project (claude.ai/design)** — the landing's DECLARED components as rendered cards, through
  the human's gate; the in-session render stays the authority (SPEC E-18).
- A new target = a new plugin section here, added through the queue like any wish.

## How it runs

1. Name the artifact's kind (it usually already stands in the queue row, SPEC T-16) and the target(s).
2. Walk the floor, then the kind's row, then each target's steps — fixing what fails BEFORE asking the
   human anything.
3. Report the walk's result in the delivery report (a stood-down publish step is named like any other,
   SPEC INV-22), then hand the human their gate with the surface ALREADY worth approving: "the README
   is current, screenshots re-shot today, forms filled — push?"

## One worked example (a skill's README, before and after the walk)

❌ *"track-coach — a compositional analysis pipeline. See `build_widget.py` for entry points; config
in the usual place. v1.4 adds INV-50 scale wording."* — fails the floor (WHAT/WHO/HOW absent, internal
vocabulary, a version claim in prose) and the skill row (no install line, no typed commands, no
when-NOT, no taste of it working).

✅ *"track-coach — a coach for music producers: point it at a track (mp3/wav/…) and an Ableton
project, get one offline page that shows where the arrangement is alive and where it stalls. Install:
`./install.sh`. Use: say 'analyse my track' with the file — deep mode runs itself. Not for mastering
metrics or loudness compliance. Below: one real read of a real track."* — the first screen answers
what/who/how in the reader's words, the commands are shown as typed, both boundary sides are stated,
and the taste comes from a real run that shows the product working.

## Work that belongs elsewhere

Reserve it for work leaving the machine: skip it for showing work in-session (communicator rule 5), for local commits, and for a prototype —
a sketch is never published, it isn't a product (base rule 16); not as a substitute for the human's

1	---
2	name: test-author
3	description: Use to derive a test matrix and write tests from a proven spec and architecture. Not a substitute for reviewing the spec itself.
4	metadata:
5	  version: 4.3.0
6	---
7	
8	# test-author — from a proven spec to tests that would have caught the bug
9	
10	> Part of the **live-spec pack** — the shared working rules (ask-never-guess · plain words, anchors trail ·
11	> one surface = one name · one home per fact · junior/senior split · checkpoints · the concurrent-edit
12	> fence · freshness · journal discipline · attic-never-delete · verify by deed · the human's gates · claims
13	> need primary sources · fix the class, sweep look-alikes · the door before code · prototype ≠ product) live ONCE in the pack's base skill, `live-spec-base` (v4.3.0), together with the
14	> settings ladder — this skill references them and elaborates only its own domain. Used standalone, this
15	> note is plain advice.
16	
17	The method was born on a real project: two user-visible bugs shipped past ~660 green tests, because
18	the facts those tests covered were pinned at the wrong LEVEL — string checks proved the code SAYS the
19	right thing while the page showed the wrong one. The rebuild that followed (the track-coach test
20	overhaul, 2026-07-02..04) produced the level ladder, the state-space walk, and the traceability
21	enforcement this skill carries. Worked patterns are paraphrased from track-coach's matrix (MIT,
22	credited); the pack's own matrix template is the shipped shape.
23	
24	**Where the paths in this file point.** Two trees are in play. The named files under `tests/`,
25	`guardrails/`, `scripts/`, and `templates/` are the live-spec pack's own, at
26	`github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. After an install, `live-spec-base` sits as a folder beside this
27	skill's folder. Every other path belongs to the project under test, starting with its `TEST_MATRIX.md`
28	and its own test folder.
29	
30	## What this skill owns
31	
32	Two artifacts, in order. **TEST_MATRIX.md** — the spec projected into a checkable grid: derived from
33	the proven spec THROUGH the proven architecture, one block per architecture node, and the spec keeps
34	sole authority over what is true. Then **the tests** — one
35	owning test per matrix row, asserting the real shipped artifact. build-pipeline keeps the order and
36	the gates; product-prover keeps semantic review; the guardrails keep mechanical enforcement. This
37	skill owns the JUDGMENT in between: which facts, at which level, asserted how.
38	
39	## Deriving the matrix (the pipeline's step 5)
40	
41	1. **Open with the artifact inventory** — every file the user receives, each owning at least one
42	   rendered-level row. An artifact nobody renders in a test can ship broken with the suite green.
43	2. **Blocks per architecture node; every spec fact ≥ 1 row.** A fact with no row is a derivation
44	   defect, found here, fixed here, always before a user could find it.
45	3. **Every row states BOTH sides** — what the fact does, and what it must never do. The never side is
46	   the regression fence: a row without it proves the happy path and nothing else.
47	4. **Every row pins a LEVEL** — the ladder below. The level is the row's most important judgment.
48	5. **Name the state space before filling cells.** Axes first: view states (mode, toggles), data
49	   states (present / absent / empty per source). A cell is element × view-state × data-state; a fact
50	   that must hold in EVERY state is an invariant and owns its own test. A flat element-by-view grid
51	   hides the data axis — the classic home of "empty shell shipped" bugs.
52	6. **Matrix-local row ids are legal, spec anchors stay the parent.** One spec fact may project into
53	   several separately-testable rows (sub-variant suffixes), and node-level mechanics (a decoder
54	   table, a gate mechanism) may carry their own contract rows. The spec anchor cited is the parent
55	   fact; an audit finding "matrix id absent from the spec" for these two kinds is expected.
56	7. **A norm-pointered clause owes a norm-conformance row.** When a spec clause carries a
57	   `norm: <path>` pointer (SPEC INV-43), the matrix owes a conformance row asserting the render's
58	   STRUCTURE against the frozen norm — every norm section and row name present in the render, no
59	   invented sections or value formats — at DOM-text level or above; the look itself stays the human's
60	   eye at the feel gate, and no pixel row claims it. The never side: a render that invents its own
61	   structure never ships green. Its sibling half lives in build-pipeline's code step — the norm-open rule
62	   with the plan-vs-prototype diff line in the delivery report — and a review cites the two halves
63	   together.
64	8. **Close by the mechanical gates, not a hand-walked list.** The coverage checklist the matrix once
65	   walked by hand retires; its facts are held mechanically at every run. The row lint
66	   (`test_matrix_rows_have_level_and_negative_side` in `tests/test_traceability.py`) reds a row that
67	   pins no level from the ladder or states no never side, naming the offending row. The generated
68	   Reference gate (`guardrails/check-matrix-reference.py`) maps every spec anchor a body row carries to
69	   its rows and reds a stale anchor no row carries, so anchor coverage and stale-reference catching are
70	   the gate's. The interface-level row per module block and the level-follows-the-layer rule (P8, P9)
71	   stay a standing suite check in `tests/test_interface_coverage.py`. The matrix `## Reference` is built
72	   by `scripts/build-matrix-reference.py` and never hand-edited — generated output, the way the spec's
73	   own code-to-location table is.
74	
75	## The level ladder — where green suites lie
76	
77	| Level | Proves | Lies about |
78	|---|---|---|
79	| string | the source or output text contains X | everything the user actually sees |
80	| DOM-text | the rendered document says X | position, visibility, color, interaction |
81	| browser-computed | real layout/style/behaviour in a real engine | subjective look and feel |
82	| pixel | the rendered look matches a frozen norm | nothing — but brittle; reserve it |
83	
84	Pinning rules: any fact about visibility, layout, color, or interaction takes browser-computed or
85	higher — a string test on such a fact is the exact class that shipped the two bugs. Content facts
86	take DOM-text. Wiring and config facts may take string, legally. Pixel is reserved for look-and-feel
87	against a frozen, approved norm. When in doubt, ask what the USER would see broken — the level must
88	be able to see the same thing.
89	
90	**The ladder is a kind-abstract shape; read the project's declared proofs, do not assume code (SPEC
91	INV-135).** The four levels above are the codebase's rungs. A project of another kind fills the ladder
92	with its own concrete proof kinds, declared at founding in the host profile's `project.proofs` line
93	(SPEC INV-36, INV-135) — a photo site's rendered level is a byte-diff of the baked output plus the
94	owner's eye-walk, a promotion campaign's is a register lint plus the owner's review, and the pack's own
95	rendered level is a string assertion against the shipped file (live-spec's matrix records that no fact
96	needs a browser-computed rung). So read the declared proof kinds before pinning levels: the rung a fact
97	takes is the project's own, and mapping every fact onto the code ladder for a non-code kind is the
98	derivation defect this reading closes.
99	
100	**The level follows the footprint's layer (SPEC INV-128).** In one line: the test level follows the layer
101	the change touches. A presentation change is asserted at browser-computed or above, because the user sees
102	it. A single-module change is asserted at its module's interface: the row asserts the module's contract.
103	It leaves the module's internals and any neighbour's render out of scope. A cross-cutting law is asserted
104	by a string or traceability test that holds across every surface it governs. Tying the level to the
105	footprint layer makes the right level a derivation rule, so the level stops being a fresh judgment call
106	each time; a presentation fact tested as a string is the exact defect the ladder exists to catch (the
107	visibility rule above — any visibility/layout/colour fact takes
108	browser-computed — is the first instance of this mapping).
109	
110	**A module's tests run against its interface; a cross-cutting law gets a test per surface (SPEC INV-101).**
111	Each module declares its interface, and each module block in the matrix owns at least one interface-level
112	row: each module's tests assert its declared interface, and they leave its internals and a neighbour's render alone.
113	A test bound to a module's internals breaks on every refactor and proves nothing about the contract; a test
114	bound to a neighbour's render couples two modules the boundary meant to separate. This gives the
115	three-question fitness test's "testable alone" [INV-122] a concrete home — one interface-level row per
116	architecture-node block. A cross-cutting law lives in the spec's declared-laws home [INV-101], is
117	enumerated once, and gets one test per surface it governs, at string or traceability level. The
118	traceability test enforces both: a declared law with a surface that has no test row goes red (the shape of
119	a spec invariant with no matrix row), and a module block with no interface-level row is a derivation defect
120	at the coverage walk (`tests/test_interface_coverage.py`).
121	
122	**The ladder tops out below the real device (SPEC INV-77).** Touch physics, scroll snapping, and
123	background throttling live past a desktop headless browser's reach — iOS ignores
124	`scroll-snap-stop`, a backgrounded tab throttles timers, momentum has no faithful emulation. A
125	behaviour living there gets a **real-device walk row**: a matrix row the suite can never turn
126	green, owed to the human's own hands on a real phone before ship — kin of the feel gate (feel is
127	the human's call, never shipped off green alone). The row states WHAT the hands check and on which
128	device class; the suite says plainly what it cannot see.
129	
130	## Writing the tests (the pipeline's step 6)
131	
132	- **Assert the real shipped artifact**: render the page, produce the file, call the function — then

142	  test removes what it creates — temp files, fixtures on disk, spawned processes, mutated shared
143	  state — and a suite run leaves the machine as it found it; a leak is a defect of the test. A
144	  test's files are born in the system temp home or the host's gitignored state dir and erased at
145	  the run's end; a user-visible folder — Downloads, Desktop, Documents — is never a test's
146	  workspace, and a headless browser's download directory is pointed at the temp home explicitly
147	  (the 42-files-in-Downloads incident, 2026-07-10). Give temp artifacts the suite's own prefix and
148	  keep one session-scoped before/after diff of the temp home in the suite, so a leak turns the run
149	  red at once, before a human eye would catch it.
150	- **A test's expected value derives independently of the code under test (SPEC INV-102).** A test
151	  compares the code's output against an expected value, and that value comes from a source other than
152	  the code under test. Never recompute the code's own formula and assert the result as the expected
153	  value; such an assertion is a mirror that can never catch the formula being wrong, since the code is
154	  only ever asserted equal to itself. Three sources are legal: a hand-computed constant, an independent
155	  derivation, or a recorded real output reviewed by a human. A round-trip or property test over the
156	  outputs stays legal, because it asserts an invariant. The ban strikes only an assertion whose
157	  expected value is produced by the same formula the code runs.
158	- **A geometry fact is asserted relative, wide, and long (SPEC INV-78).** A centering or
159	  positioning fact asserts relative geometry — the element's center within ε of the viewport's
160	  center — at two or more viewport sizes, and after N consecutive steps of the interaction, so
161	  cumulative drift shows. An absolute-pixel assertion at one viewport after one step passes forever
162	  while each next step lands further off-center.
163	- **Never edit a test to make a change pass.** A red test means the change or the matrix cell is
164	  wrong; the cell is corrected first, and the test follows the corrected cell.

166	  set. An unexpected skip (a browser missing, a fixture absent) is a failure in a quieter color.
167	- **A test passes for the same reason every run — green means deterministic (SPEC INV-155).** A test
168	  that passes on some runs and fails on others is flaky, and one question routes it: is the source of
169	  the nondeterminism removable in code the project owns, the test or the product? When it is — a
170	  dependence on wall-clock time, on test ordering, on shared or leaked state, on an unseeded random
171	  draw, on a timing assumption, or a missing wait on a tool the test drives — it is a defect fixed at
172	  its root: name the source and remove it, never a retry, a rerun-until-green, or a raised timeout that
173	  hides the race. When the tool itself misbehaves at random, with nothing to correct in the test, it is
174	  workshop noise on the problem ledger [SPEC INV-23] instead. A flake understood but not removable in
175	  one landing is quarantined by name in the pinned skip-set, marked distinct from an environment skip,

184	  dir and process group when the run's recorded owner is dead, so a killed run's orphans are swept on
185	  the next launch (and never a live concurrent run, whose owner is still alive). The harness has one canonical home —

description: Use to derive a test matrix and write tests from a proven spec and architecture. Not a substitute for reviewing the spec itself.

# test-author — from a proven spec to tests that would have caught the bug

> Part of the **live-spec pack** — the shared working rules (ask-never-guess · plain words, anchors trail ·
> one surface = one name · one home per fact · junior/senior split · checkpoints · the concurrent-edit
> fence · freshness · journal discipline · attic-never-delete · verify by deed · the human's gates · claims
> need primary sources · fix the class, sweep look-alikes · the door before code · prototype ≠ product) live ONCE in the pack's base skill, `live-spec-base` (v4.3.0), together with the
> settings ladder — this skill references them and elaborates only its own domain. Used standalone, this
> note is plain advice.

The method was born on a real project: two user-visible bugs shipped past ~660 green tests, because
the facts those tests covered were pinned at the wrong LEVEL — string checks proved the code SAYS the
right thing while the page showed the wrong one. The rebuild that followed (the track-coach test
overhaul, 2026-07-02..04) produced the level ladder, the state-space walk, and the traceability
enforcement this skill carries. Worked patterns are paraphrased from track-coach's matrix (MIT,
credited); the pack's own matrix template is the shipped shape.

**Where the paths in this file point.** Two trees are in play. The named files under `tests/`,
`guardrails/`, `scripts/`, and `templates/` are the live-spec pack's own, at
`github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. After an install, `live-spec-base` sits as a folder beside this
skill's folder. Every other path belongs to the project under test, starting with its `TEST_MATRIX.md`
and its own test folder.

## What this skill owns

Two artifacts, in order. **TEST_MATRIX.md** — the spec projected into a checkable grid: derived from
the proven spec THROUGH the proven architecture, one block per architecture node, and the spec keeps
sole authority over what is true. Then **the tests** — one
owning test per matrix row, asserting the real shipped artifact. build-pipeline keeps the order and
the gates; product-prover keeps semantic review; the guardrails keep mechanical enforcement. This
skill owns the JUDGMENT in between: which facts, at which level, asserted how.

## Deriving the matrix (the pipeline's step 5)

1. **Open with the artifact inventory** — every file the user receives, each owning at least one
   rendered-level row. An artifact nobody renders in a test can ship broken with the suite green.
2. **Blocks per architecture node; every spec fact ≥ 1 row.** A fact with no row is a derivation
   defect, found here, fixed here, always before a user could find it.
3. **Every row states BOTH sides** — what the fact does, and what it must never do. The never side is
   the regression fence: a row without it proves the happy path and nothing else.
4. **Every row pins a LEVEL** — the ladder below. The level is the row's most important judgment.
5. **Name the state space before filling cells.** Axes first: view states (mode, toggles), data
   states (present / absent / empty per source). A cell is element × view-state × data-state; a fact
   that must hold in EVERY state is an invariant and owns its own test. A flat element-by-view grid
   hides the data axis — the classic home of "empty shell shipped" bugs.
6. **Matrix-local row ids are legal, spec anchors stay the parent.** One spec fact may project into
   several separately-testable rows (sub-variant suffixes), and node-level mechanics (a decoder
   table, a gate mechanism) may carry their own contract rows. The spec anchor cited is the parent
   fact; an audit finding "matrix id absent from the spec" for these two kinds is expected.
7. **A norm-pointered clause owes a norm-conformance row.** When a spec clause carries a
   `norm: <path>` pointer (SPEC INV-43), the matrix owes a conformance row asserting the render's
   STRUCTURE against the frozen norm — every norm section and row name present in the render, no
   invented sections or value formats — at DOM-text level or above; the look itself stays the human's
   eye at the feel gate, and no pixel row claims it. The never side: a render that invents its own
   structure never ships green. Its sibling half lives in build-pipeline's code step — the norm-open rule
   with the plan-vs-prototype diff line in the delivery report — and a review cites the two halves
   together.
8. **Close by the mechanical gates, not a hand-walked list.** The coverage checklist the matrix once
   walked by hand retires; its facts are held mechanically at every run. The row lint
   (`test_matrix_rows_have_level_and_negative_side` in `tests/test_traceability.py`) reds a row that
   pins no level from the ladder or states no never side, naming the offending row. The generated
   Reference gate (`guardrails/check-matrix-reference.py`) maps every spec anchor a body row carries to
   its rows and reds a stale anchor no row carries, so anchor coverage and stale-reference catching are
   the gate's. The interface-level row per module block and the level-follows-the-layer rule (P8, P9)
   stay a standing suite check in `tests/test_interface_coverage.py`. The matrix `## Reference` is built
   by `scripts/build-matrix-reference.py` and never hand-edited — generated output, the way the spec's
   own code-to-location table is.

## The level ladder — where green suites lie

| Level | Proves | Lies about |
|---|---|---|
| string | the source or output text contains X | everything the user actually sees |
| DOM-text | the rendered document says X | position, visibility, color, interaction |
| browser-computed | real layout/style/behaviour in a real engine | subjective look and feel |
| pixel | the rendered look matches a frozen norm | nothing — but brittle; reserve it |

Pinning rules: any fact about visibility, layout, color, or interaction takes browser-computed or
higher — a string test on such a fact is the exact class that shipped the two bugs. Content facts
take DOM-text. Wiring and config facts may take string, legally. Pixel is reserved for look-and-feel
against a frozen, approved norm. When in doubt, ask what the USER would see broken — the level must
be able to see the same thing.

**The ladder is a kind-abstract shape; read the project's declared proofs, do not assume code (SPEC
INV-135).** The four levels above are the codebase's rungs. A project of another kind fills the ladder
with its own concrete proof kinds, declared at founding in the host profile's `project.proofs` line
(SPEC INV-36, INV-135) — a photo site's rendered level is a byte-diff of the baked output plus the
owner's eye-walk, a promotion campaign's is a register lint plus the owner's review, and the pack's own
rendered level is a string assertion against the shipped file (live-spec's matrix records that no fact
needs a browser-computed rung). So read the declared proof kinds before pinning levels: the rung a fact
takes is the project's own, and mapping every fact onto the code ladder for a non-code kind is the
derivation defect this reading closes.

**The level follows the footprint's layer (SPEC INV-128).** In one line: the test level follows the layer
the change touches. A presentation change is asserted at browser-computed or above, because the user sees
it. A single-module change is asserted at its module's interface: the row asserts the module's contract.
It leaves the module's internals and any neighbour's render out of scope. A cross-cutting law is asserted
by a string or traceability test that holds across every surface it governs. Tying the level to the
footprint layer makes the right level a derivation rule, so the level stops being a fresh judgment call
each time; a presentation fact tested as a string is the exact defect the ladder exists to catch (the
visibility rule above — any visibility/layout/colour fact takes
browser-computed — is the first instance of this mapping).

**A module's tests run against its interface; a cross-cutting law gets a test per surface (SPEC INV-101).**
Each module declares its interface, and each module block in the matrix owns at least one interface-level
row: each module's tests assert its declared interface, and they leave its internals and a neighbour's render alone.
A test bound to a module's internals breaks on every refactor and proves nothing about the contract; a test
bound to a neighbour's render couples two modules the boundary meant to separate. This gives the
three-question fitness test's "testable alone" [INV-122] a concrete home — one interface-level row per
architecture-node block. A cross-cutting law lives in the spec's declared-laws home [INV-101], is
enumerated once, and gets one test per surface it governs, at string or traceability level. The
traceability test enforces both: a declared law with a surface that has no test row goes red (the shape of
a spec invariant with no matrix row), and a module block with no interface-level row is a derivation defect
at the coverage walk (`tests/test_interface_coverage.py`).

**The ladder tops out below the real device (SPEC INV-77).** Touch physics, scroll snapping, and
background throttling live past a desktop headless browser's reach — iOS ignores
`scroll-snap-stop`, a backgrounded tab throttles timers, momentum has no faithful emulation. A
behaviour living there gets a **real-device walk row**: a matrix row the suite can never turn
green, owed to the human's own hands on a real phone before ship — kin of the feel gate (feel is
the human's call, never shipped off green alone). The row states WHAT the hands check and on which
device class; the suite says plainly what it cannot see.

  test's files are born in the system temp home or the host's gitignored state dir and erased at

  red at once, before a human eye would catch it.

- **A geometry fact is asserted relative, wide, and long (SPEC INV-78).** A centering or

  center — at two or more viewport sizes, and after N consecutive steps of the interaction, so
  cumulative drift shows. An absolute-pixel assertion at one viewport after one step passes forever

- **Never edit a test to make a change pass.** A red test means the change or the matrix cell is
  wrong; the cell is corrected first, and the test follows the corrected cell.
- **Pin the skip-set.** Green means zero failures AND the skip list is exactly the expected, pinned
  set. An unexpected skip (a browser missing, a fixture absent) is a failure in a quieter color.
- **A test passes for the same reason every run — green means deterministic (SPEC INV-155).** A test

  with a dated reason and an owning queue row.
- **A browser test harness launches muted and reaps what it spawned (SPEC INV-157).** A harness driving

  the pack ships it once as a template (`templates/headless_harness.py`), a consumer adopts it by

- **The suite's own plumbing must not lie (SPEC INV-80).** The skip machinery must load even on a run

  Without that early import, a broken skip would pass silently on the one machine that needed it (a `skip()` NameError once hid exactly there).

35	that skill's folder, beside this skill's folder. Every other path belongs to the project the pack is
36	attached to, including `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `JOURNAL.md`, and
37	`.live-spec/`.

39	Run every script named below from the live-spec repository root, as `python3 <path> <arguments>`. Each
40	one prints its own usage line when it is run with no arguments, so the arguments never have to be
41	guessed.

43	- **Wish** — one request a person voices in plain words, captured as a queue row.
44	- **Door** — the intake classification that sends a queued wish to one entry point of the pipeline. Its
45	  values are feature, bug, refactor, docs-only, and skip. It is decided before any code is written.
46	- **Queue row** — one row of the project's queue, `ROADMAP.md` in this pack. A closed row moves to
47	  `docs/queue-archive/`, so a row number cited below may sit there rather than in the live queue.
48	- **Lane** — one build train a session rolls through the pipeline.
49	- **Landing** — one piece of work reaching the repository's shared truth as one commit.
50	- **Host** — one project the pack attaches to. Each host keeps its own spec, queue, journal, and
51	  `.live-spec/` folder.
52	- **Host profile** — the host's own settings file, `.live-spec/profile.md`. This page reads its
53	  `project.kind`, `project.layers`, `project.design-principles`, and `project.axes` lines.
54	- **Kind** — what a host's product is, named from a fixed vocabulary: book, backend service, static
55	  site, fullstack app, CLI, or skill pack. The host profile records it.
56	- **Surface** — any part of the shipped product a user meets. A **stateful surface** holds state a
57	  user can change and find again later.
58	- **Spec-delta** — the set of spec sentences one wish or feature adds or changes.
59	- **Facet** — one aspect of a feature's design, ending as a written spec sentence.
60	- **Regression fence** — one sentence in a spec-delta naming a neighbouring promise that must stay
61	  true through the change, citing the clause it guards.
62	- **Composition axis** — one angle a stateful surface's behaviour can vary along.
63	- **Lens** — one named check the prover or the design review walks a document with.
64	- **Seat** — the session that orchestrates the work and reports to the person.
65	- **Red**, used as a verb — a check fails and stops the work at that point.

68	scenario. `[target]` marks a surface or phase the spec names and does not yet specify for build.
69	`[default]` names a value the agent chose that the person may retune. `[GAP: ...]` under a criterion

73	**The bracket codes.** `INV-`, `E-`, `T-`, `S-`, `C-`, `M-`, `D-`, `A-`, `B-`, and `ACT-` codes index
74	requirements in this pack's own `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`. Its preamble names each letter's kind: `E-` an

81	## Work that belongs elsewhere
82	
83	Reserve it for a spec the code will chase. Skip it for retro-documenting already-built code so it looks
84	specced (the spec leads, code chases), for a prototype (a sketch gets a label and a fence, never a spec),
85	for pure research notes, and for the skip-boundary edit (single file, no new behaviour — it goes straight
86	to code + its test); and reach for product-prover instead when what's wanted is a review — its half of the pair.
87	
88	## The one rule
89	
90	> A spec exists so the next reader — the prover, a teammate, or the author months later — can reason about
91	> every reachable situation. If a situation the system can reach isn't in the spec, the spec is incomplete,
92	> even if the code "works."
93	
94	## How it reads — human-first, in plain product language
95	
96	A spec is read by a **human first** (a teammate, the author months later) and a prover second — and both from
97	**one** document. Write it in the **language of the product**: plain words a product person speaks — what the
98	thing is and does, in whole sentences. Machine fragments with markup have no place in it. It doesn't have to read like a textbook/lesson either;
99	**product language is the register**, whatever fits the project. Don't fork a "readable" copy and a
100	"checkable" copy; they drift apart and one goes stale. The format below serves both at once. It was tested on a real
101	project: a prover-facing spec that read like "machine fragments with markup" was rejected by its author and
102	stopped being read, and a spec no one reads stops doing its job.
103	
104	- **The body is a list of requirements; each opens with its situation.** After the preamble and the
105	  glossary, the body is a list of requirements. A requirement is named by the situation it governs
106	  ("The spec keeps what is built apart from what is planned", "A wish is captured as a queue row that is
107	  never lost") and carries three parts in order: a **Context** block of two to four short sentences —
108	  when the situation arises, who is involved, what the reader sees; a one-sentence **User Story** — as a
109	  person in a named position, I want one thing, so that one benefit follows; and the **acceptance
110	  criteria**, the behaviour grouped into named cases. The reader meets the situation and the people in it
111	  before the first rule, and a term is introduced before a rule uses it. A person-facing requirement is
112	  also called a **scenario** — its heading carries a `[feature: F-x]` tag; a machinery or reference
113	  requirement is not a scenario.
114	- **Acceptance criteria group into named cases, one criterion carrying one trigger and one response.** A
115	  **case** is one bold line naming a situation ("**Case: a wish becomes a row at once**"), followed by two
116	  to six numbered criteria. Every criterion sits in exactly one case, and the numbering runs continuously
117	  through the requirement. The keywords *when*, *while*, *if*, *then*, and *shall* are set in lowercase
118	  italics: *shall* states a duty, *when* and *while* open a situation, *if* opens a condition and *then*
119	  its result. No word in the document is written in all capitals outside a code anchor or a filename. A
120	  guardrail holds this shape — `guardrails/check-requirement-shape.py` reds a requirement missing its
121	  Context, its User Story, or its `### Acceptance Criteria`, and a criterion whose case or anchor is wrong.
122	  The parser behind that guardrail reads fixed line forms, held in `guardrails/specformat.py`:
123	    - a requirement heading opens `## Requirement N: `;
124	    - the Context line opens `**Context:**`, and the story line opens `**User Story:**`;
125	    - the criteria sit under a `### Acceptance Criteria` heading, each one written `N. text`;
126	    - a case line reads `**Case: the situation**`, bold and alone on its line;
127	    - a glossary entry reads `- **term** — definition`.
128	- **Each scenario states how it is entered and how it exits (SPEC INV-127).** A scenario is a flow with
129	  edges, and its Context block carries them: it states how the situation arises — from which prior state,
130	  with what already true (the preconditions) — and what the situation leaves true when it resolves (the
131	  postcondition). An entry or exit that is trivially none — a top-level scenario entered from nowhere, a
132	  terminal one exiting to nowhere — is stated in one short clause, so a reader tells a decided edge from
133	  an overlooked one. The duty binds forward: a new scenario carries its edges from the first draft, and
134	  product-prover flags an existing scenario's unstated edge as a finding (its scenario-level
135	  precondition/postcondition lens, kin of the entry-symmetry lens INV-50).
136	- **The criteria carry the meaning; the machine handles stay quiet.** Every criterion is a plain sentence a
137	  person reads straight through. The short codes — `[INV-18]`, `[T-1]`, `[E-3]` — trail at the **end** of the
138	  line as quiet handles for the prover and the test matrix. A reader skims past them; the maintainer follows
139	  them. **Never open a criterion with its code.** A range such as `[T-1..T-7]` cites its whole run of codes
140	  in one anchor.
141	- **A generated code-to-location table closes the doc.** The spec closes with a `## Reference` section
142	  holding one table that maps every code its criteria carry → the requirement-and-criterion locations that
143	  carry it (for example `INV-1` → `R4.3, R4.4, R5.1`). The table is **generated output**, built from the
144	  body criteria by `scripts/build-index.py`; no one edits it by hand, and feature codes (`F-...`) live on
145	  their scenario headings and take no table row. The authored home of each code's plain statement is its
146	  criterion in the body and its noun in the glossary; the table carries locations only. The gate
147	  `guardrails/check-index-generated.py` reds a committed table that differs from a fresh build, a body code
148	  the table misses, or a table code no criterion carries — so the table can never drift into a second truth.
149	  Two commands work it. `python3 scripts/build-index.py PRODUCT_SPEC.md -o PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md` builds
150	  the table, and that output is spliced under `## Reference`. `python3
151	  guardrails/check-index-generated.py PRODUCT_SPEC.md PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md` then reads the document
152	  beside its committed copy.
153	- **Name the situation in the case; put the exact threshold in the criterion.** The bold **case** line
154	  names the situation in plain words; the numbered criteria under it carry the exact number or condition.
155	  The reader gets the shape from the case; the builder drops into the criterion for the precise value.
156	- **Use lists inside a Context block or a criterion to break up a wall of prose.** The acceptance criteria
157	  are already a numbered list by construction; this rule governs the prose around them. When a Context block
158	  or a criterion spells out several forms, legs, or arms — a label's forms, a check's three legs, a law's
159	  four arms — lay them out as bullet or numbered items so the eye scans them, and keep prose for the
160	  reasoning that connects them.
161	- **The enumeration threshold makes that checkable (SPEC INV-215).** A prose paragraph carrying an
162	  enumeration of three or more distinct, parallel facts earns bullet or numbered structure — a filename
163	  rule with its collision law and its header fields and its body parts, run together in one paragraph, is
164	  a list the reader should scan, so lay the members out as items. Prose stays for the laws, their reasoning,
165	  and their boundaries; the enumeration of parallel members becomes the list. This stays a stated writing
166	  rule, read by eye and by the prover's cognitive-load lens, and it earns no mechanical lint. A regex
167	  flagging every three-comma sentence would trip on ordinary rhetorical triads — a neutral, precise, plain
168	  register, or a rule with its actor and its reason. Telling a genuine list-owed enumeration from a
169	  rhetorical triad is a meaning call the register judge and the prover make, past a regex's reach. The rule
170	  came from the owner, 2026-07-17, reading the promoter's inter-agent design doc: a paragraph packing a
171	  filename rule, a collision law, three header fields, and four body parts belongs in a bulleted list —
172	  the human language was already right, and the one remaining fix was reading efficiency.
173	- **A preamble and a glossary open the doc.** Open the spec with a short preamble: what the document covers
174	  in two or three sentences, what the bracket codes are (each letter's kind, taken from the list under
175	  "The bracket codes" above — and that a reader can ignore them while a maintainer follows
176	  them), how the keywords *shall*, *when*, *while*, *if*, and *then* read, and that **edit history lives in
177	  the JOURNAL, apart from the spec itself.** A **glossary** follows, before the first requirement: every
178	  domain noun the body uses carries a one-sentence entry there, defined once under one name (closed
179	  vocabulary — a coined word is translated to a defined standard term before it enters the document). The
180	  gate `guardrails/check-vocabulary.py` reds a term defined twice, a glossary entry no body line uses,
181	  and a coinage listed in `guardrails/spec-coinages.json`. Its own header states what it leaves out.
182	  No script can tell a domain noun from ordinary English, so a used-but-undefined noun is caught by
183	  the cold reader instead.
184	- **The spec states the current truth — a changelog lives elsewhere.** No "changed in v0.8.3 from…" edit-history notes in the prose;
185	  the *why-we-changed-it* belongs in `JOURNAL.md` (dated, with the reason). A superseded rule may stay with a
186	  one-line "superseded by §X" pointer when the old shape still needs explaining — but the prose reads as
187	  today's truth.
188	- **Layer overview up front.** If the spec stacks layers (a credibility floor, then features on top), open
189	  with a 3–5 line "how the layers stack" map so a reader always knows where they are.
190	- **Readable-first beats terse.** Clipped machine-fragment prose gets rejected by humans as hard as a wall of
191	  fluff does. Err toward a sentence that *reads well*; keep the structure, lose the jargon. Terseness is not
192	  the goal. The goal is a headline the eye lands on, then detail it can drill into.
193	- **Write in the pack's technical-writer register.** Spec prose reads like a native-English open-source
194	  technical writer: neutral, precise, easy to follow. The full register (define abstract terms in plain
195	  words at first use, one term per concept, concrete nouns, active voice, cut nominalizations and filler,
196	  metaphors only as one-off color) and the per-section verification checklist live once in the
197	  `communicator` skill's writing register — `skills/communicator/references/writing-register.md` (its home
198	  since row 266) — spec prose follows it like every other human-facing text.
199	- **A machine gate holds the register — attention alone drifts — and the prose is written by a clean agent.**
200	  Re-styling a spec by hand drifts (a voice reads fine on a sample, then the same tells return round after
201	  round). A **tell** here is a writing habit a reader recognizes as machine-written. The durable fix has
202	  five parts, and parts 2 to 5 are proven and sealed in `docs/prose-quality-gate-design.md`:
203	    1. A fresh agent with the pack not loaded writes the prose from bare facts. A context that has
204	       loaded the pack writes ornate prose, so it only does the mechanical half. This leg is spec law
205	       (SPEC INV-84), restated in `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md`.
206	    2. `scripts/spec-style-lint.py --gate` blocks the tells a regex can see: contrast-by-denial frames,
207	       define-by-exclusion openers, jargon, shouted capitals, second person, reassurance, and future
208	       narration. Defined terms are allowlisted and marked informative regions are exempt.
209	    3. `scripts/spec-redundancy-precheck.py` catches lexical near-duplication. `scripts/spec-judge.py`
210	       then runs a fresh language-model judge against the hash-pinned rubric `scripts/judge-rubric.md`,
211	       for the redundancy and register a regex cannot see.
212	    4. An unfixed tell is recorded in `scripts/spec-waivers.json` as a dated waiver, and the running
213	       total is capped by `scripts/spec-debt-cap.json`.
214	    5. `scripts/spec-done-gate.py` is the one definition of done.
215	
216	  Restyle each section through this loop: fresh writer → gate to 0 errors → anchor multiset
217	  unchanged → suite green → re-point any broken traceability check-phrase by narrowing to a register-clean phrase
218	  (log it) → commit. The floor is the machine; the ceiling stays the exemplars + a human's read.
219	
220	This is the shape `product-prover` is tuned to read, and the one a human will actually keep open.

222	## Shipped docs state each requirement impersonally
223	
224	A shipped product doc — the spec, the test matrix, the README, a skill card — is read by everyone the project reaches: a contributor, an auditor, a future user, a reader months later. Write each requirement as three plain parts: the rule, the actor as a role (the user, the producer, the target user), and the reason it holds. The reason is load-bearing and stays; the personal attribution drops, and a dated decision keeps the date as a plain anchor and drops the name — "chosen 2026-07-06 for a cold-start reader" carries what the next reader can act on, and a person's name gives them nothing to act on.
225	
226	For that reason, personal attribution and candid process voice have one home: the local-only diaries, the JOURNAL and NEXT_STEPS, which no publish ships. Who decided a thing, and a session's own frank notes about how it went, belong there — the shipped clause carries the rule and its reason, the diary carries the story. Write the shipped clause impersonally from the first draft; do not scrub names at publish time, and let the publish floor stand only as the backstop. (SPEC INV-118.)
227	
228	## The spine — what every spec must contain (not its section order)
229	
230	The spine is a completeness checklist: it constrains what the document contains, and the section order
231	stays free. The document is organized as a glossary
232	followed by a list of requirements (per "How it reads" and `templates/PRODUCT_SPEC.template.md`); each spine
233	item lives inside a requirement's criteria, or — for a domain noun — in the glossary, and every code is
234	findable through the generated code-to-location table. Never let a new feature land without its entry.
235	
236	1. **Purpose** — why the product exists, in plain words: the opening preamble.
237	2. **Entities** — the nouns. Each defined in the **glossary**, with its attributes, its unit/valid range if
238	   it's a measure, and its **states** if it has a lifecycle. *One concept, one name* (see below).
239	3. **States & transitions** — every move an entity can make, told as criteria (which action, which actor,
240	   what triggers it). A state with no way out is a bug; say what exits it.
241	4. **Actors** — who initiates each significant action (user, role, automated service, external system).
242	   "Who does this?" must have an answer for every transition.
243	5. **Invariants** — the properties that must hold across *every* reachable state, stated as criteria that
244	   hold while the situation runs. Cover both sides:
245	   - **Safety** — what must never happen (mutually-exclusive modes, no over-claiming, no partial writes).
246	   - **Liveness** — what must eventually happen (every async path completes / times out / rolls back).
247	6. **Cross-section composition** — the part most specs miss. See the dedicated step below.
248	7. **Terms** — every domain term is defined in the glossary, once, under one name. A word of ordinary
249	   English needs no entry.
250	
251	Mark anything that needs a human's domain call with **⟨DECIDE⟩** and a one-line question. Never invent
252	intent to fill a gap — flag it.
253	
254	**Name the future with the [target] tag — it is a tripwire that drives the pipeline.** A surface or phase the
255	spec names but does not yet specify for build carries the literal tag `[target]` (the header's
256	current-vs-target paragraph lists them). That tag is the canonical, machine-checkable form of "not yet
257	specified / later surface": the pipeline's feature tripwires key off it — touching a [target] surface
258	starts at the spec step, full stop (SPEC S-0, INV-16). Plain-prose phrasings (`TBD`, "future work",
259	"planned") bind too, but always write the tag: a future the machine can't see is a future a session can
260	hand-build past the method.
261	
262	**A clause born of an approved look points at its norm (SPEC INV-43).** When the human approves a
263	visual prototype as the look ("this is the door"), the clause that encodes it carries a `norm: <path>`
264	pointer at its line end, beside its anchors — the prose carries the laws, the artifact keeps the look;
265	a build from text alone ships a cheap look-alike with a green suite (tlvphotos, 2026-07-05). Approval
266	freezes the artifact into the project's records: copy it to `docs/norms/` with a dated provenance line
267	(what, approved when, from which sketch) and point at the frozen copy, keeping the one-way fence absolute
268	— the prototype's code sits in its own named home, and nothing in the shipped product reaches into it
269	(E-17); a pointer into a live prototype home would break it. A text-born clause carries no pointer, and the law
270	binds forward — a clause owes its pointer at the first landing that touches it.
271	
272	**Reshaping an existing spec? Hold the anchor-set guard.** A restructure (a genre migration, a resection)
273	must carry exactly the prior anchor set: diff the sorted anchor list before and after — identical sets prove
274	the shape changed and no rule was lost; any delta must be a deliberate, named change. Do not renumber or
275	retire a code as a side effect of a restructure; where a rule genuinely changes home, keep its anchor and
276	state today's home.
277	
278	## The move most specs miss: compose every stateful surface across every axis
279	
280	This move catches the bugs that pass every unit test, and a feature-focused author skips it.
281	
282	When a surface (a player, a form, an editor, a panel) carries **state**, the system almost always also has
283	**global axes** it renders under. This is the **canonical axis list — its home is here; other docs point at it:**
284	
285	- **view** (compact / detailed) · **mode** (quick / full, read / edit) · **tier** · **viewport size** ·
286	  **persistence / reopen** (any state that survives a reload — localStorage, a saved file) ·
287	  **concurrency** where it applies ·
288	  **every other live surface** — every other surface that can be present at the same time, whether or not
289	  that other surface holds state: a sibling sharing the screen, or a surface the flow reaches just before
290	  or after this one (a static end screen counts). For each, state what this surface does while that one is
291	  present: hold, clear, or hand off.
292	
293	The bugs that pass every unit test live in the **product** of surface-state × axis, because each was
294	specified alone. The three authors forget most: viewport size (a grid that reflows below some width),
295	persistence/reopen (state written last session auto-restoring into a changed UI), and every other live
296	surface (a caption still naming the previous photo once the closing screen arrives, because "what the
297	caption shows when the finale is in view" was never written).
298	
299	So, for every stateful surface, before its section is called done:
300	
301	- **Enumerate it against each global axis.** For each axis value (each view/mode/tier), state what happens
302	  to the surface's state and controls. Is the state still *visible*? Still *reversible*? Does the axis
303	  transition *preserve, reset, or block* the state?
304	- **Name the composition invariant.** e.g. *"a per-stem mute/solo is reachable only while its control
305	  surface is visible; entering the compact view resets to the full mix."* Without it, the
306	  stranding bug follows: a state set in one view, hidden by another, with no way to see or undo it.
307	- **One surface, one name.** If the player's lanes and the `#stemlanes` canvas are the same thing, call
308	  them the same thing everywhere. A reviewer (human or prover) can only connect a cross-section hole when
309	  both sides are named identically and present in the same document — two names for one surface hides the
310	  seam.
311	- **If the surface persists state, compose the versions too.** When it writes localStorage/disk, enumerate
312	  version-N-1 state × version-N code explicitly: what does the current UI do when it reads a stored value
313	  that's older, partial, or belongs to a since-removed feature? State a migrate / ignore / clear rule — this
314	  is the seam behind "reopened it and it looked broken".
315	
316	## Declare the pole when a capability could live in the pack or in each host (SPEC INV-163)
317	
318	When authoring a capability the pack could hold once or each host could hold its own, declare which pole it
319	takes, so the pack↔host home is written as a decided sentence. One question decides it: can the
320	pack ship a single identical body that every host runs? When it can, the body centralizes to one pack home,
321	adopted by a package update. When the body is host-specific — it names a host's own surfaces, holds a host's
322	own data, or reads a host's own artifacts — the pack ships the shape (a template and its guidance) and each
323	host owns the instance it fills. Write the chosen pole into the clause and cite the split [INV-163]; the duty
324	binds forward [INV-159], so a new host-specific capability names its pole from the first draft while the
325	bodies that predate the clause stand as they are cited.
326	
327	## The feature delta, assembled — one home for its mandatory parts
328	
329	Author in this order; every part below is mandatory for a feature and no scope cut may trim it
330	(scope dials richness; it never trims the safety net — SPEC T-15):
331	
332	1. **Regression fences** — when the wish touches a live surface (next section; SPEC T-14, INV-19);
333	2. **The new behaviour itself** — entities, states, transitions, composed across the canonical axes;
334	3. **The standard-facet sweep** — every facet a spec sentence, decided or `[default]`-tagged (SPEC T-13, INV-18);
335	4. **The fit walk** — how the feature sits in the person's path, kind-scaled (SPEC INV-29);
336	5. **The two closing sentences** — non-goals + one success measure (SPEC INV-20, INV-21).
337	
338	A delta missing any numbered part is incomplete at authoring time — the author catches it before the prover ever sees it.
339	
340	## The regression fences — run first when the wish touches a surface that already lives (SPEC T-14, INV-19)
341	
342	Before authoring anything new, preserve the neighbours. The spec-delta opens with one sentence per
343	existing promise that must stay true through the change ("the catalog still opens on click"), each
344	citing the spec clause it guards. A fence is not new law and earns no new matrix row — the cited
345	clause's row already carries its never-side, and the landing's full-suite run is what proves the fence
346	held. Split what the delta touches: promises that stay are fenced; behaviour being changed is
347	re-authored as new law — a fact is fenced or re-authored, never both. A fence that finds no clause
348	behind it has discovered an unwritten promise: reconcile it from the shipped truth (like an adopted
349	claim), write it as its own spec fact with its own row, and state it explicitly. If
350	the cited neighbour claim is adoption-born and still unverified, its reconciliation runs before it can
351	be fenced — a hope cannot be fenced. Name the fences by cited anchor in the wish's queue row, which is
352	a row of `ROADMAP.md` in this pack ("fences: …"), so "untouched and still true" stays searchable. A
353	prototype fences nothing — it promises
354	nothing.
355	
356	## The facet sweep — run when a wish's door says feature (SPEC T-13, INV-18)
357	
358	A person asks for a feature in the words they have; the dimensions below exist whether or not anyone
359	names them ("add a room where photos hang" never says "and decide what happens on a phone"). When the
360	door says feature, drafting the spec-delta walks this checklist — the **canonical facet list; its home is
361	here**, one list for every project.
362	
363	**Read the project's declared layers, do not assume code (SPEC INV-135).** Which surfaces a facet sweep
364	reaches, and what a footprint's layer means for this project, come from the host profile's declared
365	`project.layers` line (SPEC INV-36, INV-135) — a photo site's layers are content, rendering engine, and
366	deployment, a campaign's are message, channels, and assets, and the pack's own are the rulebook, the
367	working skills, and the guardrails. The facet dimensions below are kind-abstract; read the declared

482	sits in the person's path — the questions nobody thinks to ask until a guest is stuck at the tenth
483	picture with no way on (tlvphotos, 2026-07-06). **The lens lists' home is here**, kind-scaled, curated
484	with incidents exactly like the facet list:
485	
486	- **product / UX kind — the visitor's journey:** how does the person arrive here (every entry door,
487	  including the ones past the main one) · what do they do here · where do they go NEXT from every state this surface
488	  can be in (no dead ends — the door↔room loop incident, tlvphotos 2026-07-06) · what does a return
489	  visit change (seen-state, no-repeat — and the remembered state it implies) · a conditionally-entered
490	  face (first visit, empty state, onboarding, a one-time banner) names its deliberate re-entry path or
491	  states the one-way as a decision (SPEC INV-50) · what does the feel owe

493	- **infra / backend kind — the flows:** inputs → outputs · the data's lifecycle (created, updated,
494	  stale, gone) · every failure path and what the caller sees;
495	- **skill kind — the behaviour:** the trigger · the correction it makes · when it must not fire.

497	The walk interrogates the feature, never the person (SPEC INV-29): derive answers from the existing
498	spec and shipped truth; close the trivially-closable holes and write how each was closed;

502	## The delta's two closing sentences — non-goals and the success measure (SPEC INV-20, INV-21)
503	
504	Every feature's spec-delta closes with two short sentences, always written; neither may be
505	left out. **Non-goals**: what is deliberately left out ("version comparison waits for a later pass");
506	"nothing deliberately left out this time" is itself valid — only a missing sentence is a hole, and a
507	non-goal that narrows what the wish asked for rides the batched report, never a silent narrowing.
508	**A success measure**: how we'd notice the feature worked for its person, a number where one exists;
509	decided or `[default]`-tagged — the tag marks provenance only, no test row derives from it until the
510	reading machinery lands. The quantification questions (analytics tag? how measured? A/B worth it?) ride
511	the facet sweep's batched report. Both bind forward; an adopted feature owes its pair at the first
512	landing that touches it. A prototype writes neither — it promises nothing.
513	
514	## The primary unit — one per project type, traced end to end (SPEC E-29, INV-73)
515	
516	A spec has a primary unit: the thing the reader counts, the product's spine repeated. The unit is a
517	parameter of the project's type — the way a domain swaps a template — declared once, then it sets the
518	heading style, the acceptance-criterion shape, and what the coverage check means.
519	
520	| project type | primary unit | the coverage check validates |
521	|---|---|---|
522	| web / app | a user-facing **feature** (a visible flow) | every feature → architecture node(s) + a test |
523	| CLI / library / API | a **command** / function / endpoint | every surface → its contract, an owning module + a test |
524	| methodology package | a rule or **guarantee** the pack promises | every guarantee → an enforcing mechanism (a script, a gate, a template) |
525	| content / book / article | an **argument** / chapter / section | every promised argument → a home in the outline (a structure check; no technical architecture) |
526	
527	**The mechanic is one, for every type.** Each unit carries a stable inline tag on its heading — the same
528	family as the anchors, e.g. `[feature: F-wish]` — and the downstream artifacts back-reference it: one
529	coverage table in ARCHITECTURE.md names the implementer node(s) and a test per unit. The two-way check reads
530	both directions — every unit has an implementer and a test, and every promised unit carries its tag. In this
531	pack that check is the feature-coverage trace in `tests/test_traceability.py`, reading ARCHITECTURE.md's
532	`## Feature coverage` table. This
533	is the anchor-ownership machinery extended a level up, never a second machine to keep in sync.
534	
535	**No file explosion.** One PRODUCT_SPEC.md, one ARCHITECTURE.md, one TEST_MATRIX.md; the unit tags live
536	inline in the prose and the one coverage table binds them. Shard into per-feature files only for a
537	genuinely huge project, and only by explicit call.
538	
539	**The source is plain Markdown; the render resolves the links.** The source stays plain Markdown — a
540	tag plus one table. When a doc is rendered, a relative `.md` cross-link opens its rendered `.html`
541	neighbour and its `#anchor` lands on the target heading (ROADMAP row 195, shipped 2026-07-10). Linking
542	a trailing bracket code to its row in the code-to-location table stays an optional later leg; until that lands, a reader
543	follows a bare tag by searching the source.
544	
545	**On live-spec itself.** live-spec is a package, but its scenarios are the product's features, so it
546	dogfoods the web/app row: each person-facing scenario heading tags `[feature: F-x]` and the Feature
547	coverage table maps it to its skills and its test. The machines that work behind the scenes (guardrails,
548	host contract) implement guarantees; they are not user-facing features, and they stay outside the feature layer
549	by the type's own definition of its unit. The decided design note is `docs/spec-format-by-project-type.md`.
550	
551	**The heading convention makes the reverse direction mechanical (SPEC INV-132).** For the two-way check to
552	catch a scenario whose tag was forgotten, an untagged heading has to be unambiguous — and it is not on its
553	own, since the checker cannot tell a new scenario missing its tag from a machinery or reference section
554	that never had one. So every requirement heading — `## Requirement N: …`, the level every person-facing
555	scenario uses — carries either its `[feature: F-x]` tag (a person-facing scenario) or the explicit
556	`[not a scenario]` marker (a machinery, rules, or reference section, legitimately untagged), and an
557	untagged, unmarked requirement heading is unambiguously red. The parts under it — the `### Acceptance
558	Criteria` sub-heading and the bold case lines — nest inside a requirement already tagged or marked, so they
559	owe nothing. When a section that is not a person-facing scenario is added, state its `[not a scenario]`
560	marker in the same edit — a new machinery heading that passes silently is the gap this closes.
561	
562	## The content contract — when a generic engine is extracted from an instance (SPEC INV-79)
563	
564	A generic engine carved out of a working project inherits the donor's assumptions silently: an id
565	format, a hardcoded wordmark, a path, a language default. At extraction the spec opens a **content
566	contract** section: every donor-specific constant the extraction finds becomes a named entry — what
567	the engine requires from any instance's content, in the engine's own vocabulary — and each entry
568	owes a test that the engine works without the donor's value (test-author's half of the same law).
569	An assumption with no entry is a leak the next instance discovers in production.
570	
571	## Crossing the instance→engine boundary — provenance and naming (SPEC INV-119)
572	
573	A feature usually proves itself first on a live instance and then generalizes into the engine. When that history goes into the engine's spec, write it as the engine's own record: the reader is anyone who runs the engine, so every provenance handle points at something that reader can reach, and the spec reads as generic from the first line.
574	
575	Four conventions carry the boundary:
576	
577	- **The history reads as a reconciliation.** Head the history section "Reconciliation log — how each behaviour landed in code", and let each entry trace a behaviour to where it landed in the engine's own code. This is a spec-versus-code reconciliation the engine's reader can follow. It is not a fork's delta against an instance's reference implementation.
578	- **Provenance cites the engine's own public commit.** Each entry names where the behaviour landed in the engine — "landed in engine commit `<hash>`" — a commit any reader can check out in the engine's own history. A private instance's commit is invisible to that reader, so an instance hash stays out of the engine's provenance.
579	- **One intro sentence states the normal intake path, once.** Open the log with a single sentence naming the usual route — "Most rows record a feature proven first on a live instance and then generalized into the engine" — so no per-entry line re-explains where features come from.
580	- **A mechanism carries a neutral internal name; a visible instance label is marked as instance copy.** Name a mechanism by what it does in the engine's own vocabulary — "the unfold step", "the show-more control". Where a running instance shows locale-specific words for it, the spec notes that string as instance-supplied copy the instance plugs in [INV-79], and the neutral term stays the mechanism's one name [E-4].
581	
582	## Standard vocabulary — what our house terms map to
583	
584	The pack's method is its own, but its concepts are the field's, and naming the lineage lets a reader who
585	knows requirements engineering recognize what a live-spec document is doing. The crosswalk to the field's
586	vocabulary (`ISO`/arc42/C4) lives in `docs/spec-format-by-project-type.md`.
587	
588	Two boundaries the crosswalk does not erase: our spec stays a single requirements-genre document — a
589	glossary and a body of requirements — and a term joins our vocabulary only when it is measurable or
590	verifiable here, never for the borrowed authority alone.

592	## How spec-author works
593	
594	1. **Author / grow the relevant requirement** in `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`: find (or open) the requirement the
595	   change belongs to — the intake placement verdict made real: the scenario is the wish's place on
596	   the feature map (SPEC INV-37) — and grow its Context, its User Story, and its named-case criteria, plain
597	   language, anchors at line-ends. Add any new domain noun to the glossary in the same edit. The
598	   code-to-location table is regenerated at freeze by `scripts/build-index.py`; leave it to the builder
599	   rather than editing it by hand. Reuse the existing vocabulary; don't introduce a second word for an existing concept.
600	   Starting fresh? Copy `templates/PRODUCT_SPEC.template.md`. (Template paths resolve from the pack repo —
601	   github.com/happysasha18/live-spec. A standalone install of this skill reads them from a checkout of
602	   that repository, taken with `git clone https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. They are
603	   deliberately not copied into the skill dir: the pack is the source, a copy would fork the truth.)
604	2. **Ask, don't silently fill.** When the spec needs a decision only the author can make (a threshold, a
605	   policy, desired behavior on an edge), ask the leading question or mark ⟨DECIDE⟩, treating intent as
606	something to confirm; never infer it.
607	3. **Run the completeness pass** (below) on the section just written.
608	4. **Hand off to `product-prover` on the whole spec — the delta included.** The prover catches a
609	   cross-section hole only when *both* sides of the seam are in the document; a surface added in
610	   isolation, or left unlinked, is invisible to it. So re-prove the whole spec whenever a surface is added.
611	5. **Then walk the two layers to the tests** — the architecture doc (nodes owning the spec's facts,
612	   proven with the architecture lens), then the matrix derived node × fact (`spec → prove → architecture
613	   → prove architecture → matrix → test → code`; build-pipeline owns the steps). The spec leads; code
614	   chases it.
