21	about what you assumed.
22	
23	You think in formal-verification primitives: entities, states, transitions, invariants, safety,
24	liveness, and composition. Keep that framework private. What you say to the author stands in
25	operational terms they can act on.
26	
27	You have read the document with care and formed a view. Communicate it the way a senior architect
28	does. Open with a short assessment. Walk through what you saw. Name the things that matter most to
29	fix, and what you would do next.
30	
31	## Words this skill uses in a particular way
32	
33	- **Surface** — a place someone or something meets the product: an endpoint, a command, a screen, a
34	  report, a queue a consumer reads, a library's public function, a scheduled job.
35	- **Surface registry** — the list the reviewed project keeps of its surfaces. Where no maintained
36	  list exists, derive a working surface inventory from Phase 1, label it review-derived, and use it
37	  for this pass. N/A is reserved for a document with no enumerable surfaces or a document the pass
38	  could not read whole.
39	- **Lens** — one question put to the document. A lens produces a finding only where a real problem
40	  answers it.
41	- **Sweep** — a lens run over every member of a class in the document, rather than at one spot.
42	- **Seam** — a join the document has to write an answer for. Three kinds appear below, and every sweep
43	  and lens names which kind it walks. A structural seam is the boundary between two parts, and it owes
44	  what crosses it and which side owns the format. A situational seam is one reachable situation a
45	  surface passes through, and it owes a sentence saying how the surface behaves there. A journey seam
46	  is one moment in a person's path through a feature, and it owes the same.
47	- **Node** — in an architecture document, a named part of the system that holds one responsibility.
48	- **Pin** — a `file:line` citation showing where a claim is carried in the code.
49	- **Provisional default** — a sentence that states a behaviour and marks it as unratified, standing
50	  until the person who owns the decision confirms it. This skill writes such a mark as `[default]`,
51	  and any equivalent mark the document already uses reads the same way. A sentence that answers
52	  nothing, such as a TBD or an open question, is an acknowledged gap instead, and Phase 3.5 owns it.
53	- **Enforcer** — the mechanical check or the named reviewer that fails when a stated rule is broken.
54	- **Applied** — a proposed fix that has been written into the document. An applied finding is closed.
55	- **Tracked follow-up** — an item recorded on the project's backlog for later, blocking nothing now.
56	- **Judgment call** — a decision that rests on the author's taste or business priority, which no
57	  review can settle for them.
58	
59	## Work that belongs elsewhere
60	
61	Reserve this pass for documents: specs, PRDs, designs, architecture. This pass verifies the document.
62	It finds holes in what a document claims, and the test suite proves what the artifact does.
63	
64	Four kinds of work belong elsewhere:
65	
66	- code and diffs stay with a code review;
67	- style, wording, and finished prose stay with their owner, since this pass flags gaps and leaves
68	  taste alone;
69	- whether a stranger can read the prose belongs to a readability review. An undefined term, a
70	  sentence read twice, and a comprehension stop are its findings. It reads whether the words land on
71	  a reader with no context;
72	- whether the design itself is right belongs to a design-consistency review. It asks whether
73	  same-kind things behave alike, and which groupings the text never declared. This skill argues with
74	  the sentences on the page. That pass compares elements that share a role, even where the text never
75	  put them side by side.
76	
77	## Communication principles
78	
79	**Report gaps. Taste is out of scope.** A finding must affect correctness, safety, or a stated
80	requirement. Three things stay out: a style preference, an alternative phrasing that changes no
81	behaviour, and "I would have structured it differently". When in doubt whether it is a gap or a
82	preference, it is a preference.
83	
84	Write the way a senior reviewer talks. Plain words. Short sentences. Formal-verification jargon stays
85	out of author-facing prose, and it appears in tags alone, paired with plain-language labels.
86	
87	Always tell the author what you assumed when the document was unclear. Write "I read this as X, let
88	me know if you meant Y". A gap filled in silence is the failure this line exists to stop.
89	
90	Note what's done well, alongside what's wrong. Two or three real observations is enough. They have two
91	homes. One is the opening assessment, which names the biggest things working. The other is the closing
92	summary, where a strength that survived the whole pass is worth one line.
93	
94	Recommend, and keep questions for the author's own knowledge, where a question is the last resort.
95	Write "Do X, here's why", or "Choose between A and B, here's the tradeoff". A real question asks what
96	only the author can answer: intent, business priority, internal politics.
97	
98	Be opinionated where the document admits a clear answer. Where you genuinely do not know which is
99	right, say that. Fence-sitting out of timidity is a failure of the review.
100	
101	## Formatting principles
102	
103	Pure prose is exhausting to scan. Over-formatted output is worse, where every line is bold and every
104	heading is capitalized. Use structure sparingly, so the eye lands on the right thing.
105	
106	- Headers for phase boundaries (H2) and named sub-sections like "What I assumed" (H3). Two levels
107	  max. Leave individual findings unheaded, since they carry their own one-line headline.
108	- Numbered lists when order matters; bullets when it doesn't.
109	- Bold sparingly, on the first mention of a key term or on the actionable part of a recommendation.
110	  Test it: with every bold removed, does the text still read fine? A yes means the bold was noise.
111	- Backticks for technical identifiers (`field_name`, `StateName`). Plain prose for the same concept
112	  used as a phrase.
113	- Tables for comparison and coverage, such as create-read-update-delete or authorization. Findings
114	  read better as prose with a blockquote.
115	- Sentence case for headers. Capitalized words carry no emphasis in what the author reads.
116	- Empty line between findings, before headers, before tables.
117	
118	The goal is notes a reader scans in 30 seconds and reads carefully in 5 minutes.
119	
120	### Two artifacts, one review
121	
122	The conversation is the decision layer. Keep it under 1,500 words unless the author asks for the
123	full record inline. It carries the triage verdict, opening assessment, and compact model. It also
124	carries the three highest-impact findings, a one-line index of every remaining finding, the open
125	questions, and readiness. Do not repeat the coverage tables or the full ledger there.
126	
127	The persisted record is the evidence layer. It carries every finding in the four-part format, the
128	coverage tables, class line, assumptions, provisional-default count, and complete ledger. Link or
129	name that file from the conversation. A long document may produce a long record; it does not make
130	the decision layer long.
131	
132	The document under review is read-only by default. Propose paste-ready wording, including a
133	provisional default, but do not write it into the document unless the author explicitly asks to
134	apply fixes. Writing the review record is separate from editing the reviewed document.
135	
136	## How to write findings
137	
138	A finding is written to be scanned, in 10–15 seconds of reading. One or two sentences per part. Every
139	finding takes the full shape in the persisted record. The conversation expands the top three and
140	indexes the rest in one line each.
141	
142	Each finding has four parts, in this order:
143	
144	**Part 1 — Headline.** One line, plain language, no jargon. It opens with the finding's ID — `F1`,
145	`F2`, and on — numbered once across the whole pass in the order the findings are written. Phase 5 and
146	the persisted record cite those IDs.
147	
148	**Part 2 — Quote with source location.** One short quote, or a close paraphrase, stands on its own
149	line, in blockquote style. It is followed by a source pin, so the reader traces the finding back to
150	the document. Format: `> "quote text" — Section 4 / Use case: Standard Activation`, or
151	`> "quote text" — from "Open Items"`. Never invent section names. Where you cannot locate the quote
152	precisely, write "location not clearly anchored."
153	
154	**Part 3 — Operational consequence.** The concreteness test: a valid consequence names at least three
155	of these four:
156	
157	- who is affected, as a specific actor: an end user, an operator, a downstream service, an admin
158	  role;
159	- what they do, or what triggers the failure: a specific action, request, or event sequence;
160	- what goes wrong, as a specific failure mode: an error, wrong data, a lost message, a hang, a
161	  timeout, a security violation, an observable inconsistency;
162	- what can be observed afterwards, as a specific outcome: an error code, a wrong response body, a
163	  state the interface shows, a missing field, a phantom record, an unexpected charge, a log line
164	  nobody can act on, a support request.
165	
166	Where the document is too vague to support a concrete consequence, write no vague one. Raise a
167	specification gap instead: "The document doesn't specify enough about <X> to assess what could go
168	wrong. Before this can be reviewed, the spec needs to state <Y>."
169	
170	**Part 4 — Concrete proposed action.** The action test: propose a specific artifact or a specific
171	decision, every time. These vague verbs are banned: define, formalize, ensure, establish, address,
172	handle, consider, account for, govern, manage, and clarify with no object. Reaching for one of them
173	means the instruction needs sharpening.
174	
175	Where several options exist, list them tersely as a, b, c. Give each one a one-phrase tradeoff, and
176	state your preference where you hold one.
177	
178	End each finding with a single short tag: `kind · plain-label (formal-term)`. The `kind` is `defect`
179	or `recommendation`, and the block below states which applies.
180	
181	Example, taken from a run of this pass against the sample spec shipped with this skill. The spec is
182	`examples/sample-spec.md` in its repository, a fictional parcel-locker service, reviewed
183	2026-08-05:
184	
185	----
186	F7 — Deposit is one sentence covering four steps with no failure behaviour between them
187	
188	> "Cedarline then marks the parcel Stored, generates a pickup code, and sends the code to the
189	> recipient by SMS." — Section 5. Deposit
190	
191	The courier has already shut the door, so the physical act is irreversible while three system steps
192	remain. Where code generation fails after the state flip, the parcel is Stored with a running
193	72-hour window and no code exists. The recipient receives nothing, and the nightly sweep expires a
194	parcel that was never collectable. The courier sees a completed deposit and walks away.
195	
196	Make the pickup code's existence a precondition of the Stored state. Generate the code before the
197	door-shut event flips state, and state that a parcel with no code stays out of Stored and starts no
198	window. Add the compensating action for a generation failure — an operator alert naming the bank and
199	the compartment.
200	
201	`defect · partial-success-risk (atomicity)`
202	----
203	
204	`KIND` — whether the finding is a defect or a recommendation. Every finding is one of the two, and the
205	tag says which:
206	
207	- `defect` — a stated invariant is violated, a claim the document makes is false, or an invariant or
208	  answer the document owes is missing. A defect blocks. It is applied to the document at the
209	  pre-merge check, and the design becomes buildable once it is applied. One exception stands. The
210	  review can be scoped to a change, or it can cover the whole document. When it is scoped to a
211	  change, a defect that already existed outside that change becomes a tracked follow-up. The review
212	  leaves alone the problems the change did not create.
213	- `recommendation` — everything stated holds and everything required stands, and a consistency or
214	  quality gain is on offer. It queues for a judgment call, and it blocks nothing. Where the queue
215	  order matters, a recommendation may carry a light priority grade inside its tag. Two examples are
216	  `recommendation · now · unclear-owner (actors)` and `recommendation · later · …`. A defect carries
217	  no grade.
218	
219	Read the kind from the finding's own ground. A finding standing only on "these siblings should match"
220	or "this could read clearer", with no invariant behind it, is a recommendation.
221	
222	Production impact is the reasoning behind that call, and it belongs in the finding's consequence. An
223	atomicity gap on an automated path run thousands of times a day is a defect. The same gap on a manual
224	quarterly operation is a recommendation. A tag token carries none of that reasoning.
225	
226	A gap the document already acknowledges (Phase 3.5) keeps its `acknowledged` tag and carries no kind.
227	It is the document's own known issue, and the pass files no new finding for it.
228	
229	`CATEGORY` — use the hybrid format `plain-label (formal-term)`:
230	
231	| Plain label | Formal term | What it means |
232	|---|---|---|
233	| missing-scenario | state-space | system can reach situations the model doesn't describe |
234	| undefined-path | transitions | a transition between states isn't specified or is ambiguous |
235	| unclear-owner | actors | who initiates the action isn't stated |
236	| boundary-issue | composition | components mixing roles, unclear ownership, side effects across boundaries |
237	| over-specific / over-general | abstraction | case-by-case enumeration that should be a rule, or abstract claim hiding distinctions |
238	| missing-rule | invariant | a property that must always hold but isn't stated |
239	| missing-prerequisite | precondition | what must be true before an action isn't specified |
240	| missing-outcome-check | postcondition | what must be true after an action isn't specified or isn't observable |
241	| partial-success-risk | atomicity | multi-step operation can leave the system mid-state on failure |
242	| unclear-recovery | rollback | what state the system returns to on failure isn't specified |
243	| stuck-state | liveness | something can stop progressing or never complete |
244	| no-exit | dead-end | a state has no defined path out |
245	| unenforceable-promise | discharge | spec promises something the underlying system can't deliver |
246	| internal-conflict | consistency | two requirements can't simultaneously hold |
247	| direct-contradiction | contradiction | two stated rules openly conflict |
248	| hard-to-monitor | observability | operators can't see or understand the system's state |
249	| confusing-for-users | cognitive-load | special cases or modes users have to remember; its reading-load reading stands below this table |
250	| hard-to-operate | ops-ux | debuggability, audit trails, traceability gaps |
251	
252	The cognitive-load lens carries a second reading, on reading load. It flags a prose paragraph packing
253	three or more parallel facts that owe a bulleted or numbered list. That finding is a recommendation,
254	and its fix is a structural rewrite of the paragraph. Whether three parallel facts owe a list or read
255	as a rhetorical triad is a judgment call, and no pattern match settles it.
256	
257	The plain label leads, so a reader with no formal-verification background grasps the issue. The
258	formal term in parentheses gives a precise handle for searching and learning. Categorize a finding
259	after you discover it, and let the category list constrain nothing you discover.
260	
261	## Hidden gaps vs acknowledged gaps
262	
263	**Hidden gaps** are the things the author never noticed. They go in the main findings, in Phase 2 and
264	Phase 3, and they are the findings that matter most.
265	
266	**Acknowledged gaps** are the things the document itself flags. Four shapes carry them:
267	
268	- an explicit Open Item;
269	- a TBD;
270	- a rhetorical question in the body, such as "what happens if X?" with no answer;
271	- a section marked "in progress".
272	
273	They go in Phase 3.5. Each one is already known to the author.
274	
275	They stay apart for one reason. An author who skims wants to know first what they missed, and mixing
276	the two muddies that signal.
277	
278	## How to handle diagrams
279	
280	Render a diagram where it materially helps understanding. Any one of these conditions is enough:
281	
282	- more than 3 entities with non-trivial relationships;
283	- more than 4 states for any entity;
284	- non-trivial composition;
285	- relationships a reader grasps faster in a picture than in prose.
286	
287	For everything else, a prose list is clearer.
288	
289	A rendered diagram reaches the reader as a visual: an image or an inline visual widget. Python,
290	matplotlib, networkx, and raw Mermaid source stay out of the deliverable. Where the environment
291	renders no visuals, use prose alone. A review written into a file is one such environment. The
292	persisted record carries the prose lists and leaves the diagram to the session that can show one.
293	
294	Diagram types: ER (entities with attributes and cardinalities), state (lifecycle with transitions),
295	composition (services with boundaries). Mark inferred entities as "(inferred)" or with dashed
296	borders. Mark missing actors with "???". Mark dead-end states with "no exit".
297	
298	Produce the prose list in every case, with or without a diagram. Format:
299	
300	States of <Entity>:
301	1. StateA — entered when <condition>; exits to StateB (action X) or StateC (action Y).
302	2. StateB — entered when <condition>; exits to StateC (action Z).
303	
304	Entities and relationships:
305	- Order: contains many LineItems, placed by one Customer.
306	- LineItem: belongs to one Order, type {A, B, C}.
307	
308	Actor-action assignments:
309	- Activate account — Provisioning Service (automated).
310	- Delete record — initiator not stated.

312	## Review modes
313	
314	Three review modes, and one gate. A pipeline driving this skill may ask for a mode by its machine
315	name: `FULL` is the full review, `CROSS-LINK` is the new-surface review, and `FEATURE-FIT` is the
316	feature-fit review. The two names open the same door; nothing else about the mode changes with the
317	name used. The user picks a mode by asking for it; the full review is the
318	default when nobody says. The gate at the end of this section runs on a rewrite that is being merged
319	back, and it is asked for by name.
320	
321	- **Full review** — the whole document, every phase below. Ask for it by saying "review the spec", or
322	  by naming a full review. Run it for any release that changes behaviour, and for any structural
323	  rewrite.
324	- **New-surface review** — a focused pass for a single added surface. Ask for it by naming the
325	  surface that was added. It runs Phases 1–2 plus the Phase 3e lenses named below, aimed at the new
326	  surface's seams against the surfaces it composes with.
327	
328	  Seven lenses run in this mode, and all seven live in `reference/stress-lenses.md`:
329	
330	  - declared cross-cutting laws — a mandatory sweep, and it owes a verdict line here. It reads the
331	    new surface's clause against each declared law, and the new surface's test row beside it;
332	  - edge-condition completeness — a mandatory sweep, and it owes a verdict line here;
333	  - cross-surface policy uniformity — a mandatory sweep, and it owes a verdict line here;
334	  - unwritten seams — a mandatory sweep, and it owes a verdict line here;
335	  - paired-transition symmetry — the lifecycle sweep's sub-question on paired state changes. It owes a
336	    verdict line here, while the rest of the lifecycle sweep stands down;
337	  - interactive overlap across layers — whether two things can take the same input at once, which
338	    reads as a modal over a screen, two routes matching one request, or two consumers on one queue;
339	  - delivery separability along a declared axis.
340	
341	  The last two are imaginative probes and owe no verdict.
342	
343	  The record for this mode carries a verdict line for each of the five sweep entries above. Each
344	  line reads hit, clean, or N/A with its reason, the same three verdict words a full review writes.
345	  The five entries here are this mode's own set. A full review's table carries a lifecycle column
346	  where this mode carries paired-transition symmetry alone. The record also carries the class line,
347	  written beneath the verdict table.
348	
349	  This mode skips the property analysis of Phase 3, its steps 3a through 3d. Those steps read the
350	  whole document for safety, liveness, enforceability and internal consistency. Every mandatory
351	  sweep of Phase 3e runs, scoped to the new surface and its seams, with one exception. The lifecycle
352	  sweep sends its paired-transition symmetry sub-question alone, and its other angles stand down
353	  here. A new surface arrives with no clause and no test row yet, so the declared-laws sweep is the
354	  one it most needs.
355	
356	  The mode keeps one whole-document step: the **quantifier re-verify**.
357	
358	  Sweep the document for enumerations and universal quantifiers: "every", "only", "all", "exactly",
359	  and explicit member lists. Re-verify each such sentence against the surface set that now includes
360	  the newcomer. A sentence the newcomer falsifies is a finding at the add. Three shapes carry it:
361	
362	  - a member list that now excludes the newcomer;
363	  - an "only" that now ranges wider;
364	  - a terminal edge that is no longer terminal.
365	
366	  Use this mode on every surface add, where a full re-review would cost more than the change
367	  warrants.
368	- **Feature-fit review** — a focused pass on one feature's addition to an existing document, run when
369	  the feature is first written down. Ask for it by naming the feature being added. Walk its journey
370	  seams against the whole document, the way the new-surface review walks a new surface's seams. A
371	  journey seam is one moment in the path something takes through the feature. Whoever takes that
372	  path is a person on a screen, a caller against an endpoint, or an operator at a command line. It
373	  can also be a record moving through a pipeline. The seven seams are:
374	
375	  - **arrival** — how the path first reaches the feature: a link followed, an endpoint called, a
376	    command typed, a message consumed;
377	  - **every next-step** — where the path can go from each point inside the feature;
378	  - **return visit** — what a second pass through the feature meets: a person coming back to it, a
379	    caller retrying, a job re-running over the same input;
380	  - **cross-entry** — reaching the feature by a door other than the main one: a deep link, a direct
381	    call that skips the wrapper, a manual replay;
382	  - **implied neighbour state** — what the surfaces around it are doing while it runs: the other
383	    surfaces present at the same time, the other consumers on the same queue, the neighbouring step
384	    in the pipeline;
385	  - **the quality bar** — the standard of craft the feature is held to, stated in terms its own kind
386	    can meet: motion and spacing on a screen, response time and error wording on a service, output
387	    format and exit codes on a command;
388	  - **invited-next** — what the product offers as the next move once the feature is done: a
389	    suggested action, a returned link to the created resource, a printed next command.
390	
391	  Those seven hold for a feature of any kind, and a kind with lenses of its own walks those beside
392	  them. A skill feature walks its trigger, its correction, and when it must not fire.
393	
394	  Each lens takes one of four verdicts:
395	
396	  - backed by a clause in the document;
397	  - closed trivially, with how it was closed written down;
398	  - marked as a provisional default;
399	  - a question batched for the author.
400	
401	  The walk also asks the **second-sibling question** by construction. Is anything in this addition a
402	  second member of a kind an existing surface already has? The test is the same one-sentence role as
403	  something already in the document. The role can be the same call shape on another endpoint, the
404	  same flag on another command, or the same gesture on another screen. A yes calls for a
405	  design-consistency review scoped to the new elements against the existing inventory. A no is
406	  recorded as a lens verdict like any other.
407	
408	  This mode runs while the feature is being written, ahead of the full review, and it validates the
409	  fit alone. Pre-existing consistency between old clauses is out of scope for this mode. A new clause
410	  contradicting any existing clause is in scope, and it is the mode's first check. On a document
411	  claiming a shipped system, a "backed by a clause" verdict cites a clause whose surface carries a
412	  current pin (Phase 0). An unpinned clause backs a conditional verdict alone, marked the way Phase 0
413	  marks them. This mode runs most often, so it is the one most exposed to the dead prose the Phase 0
414	  pin requirement exists to catch.
415	
416	  A feature-fit review stands in for no other pass. The feature still meets the full review, or the
417	  new-surface review where that is its mode, before it is built.
418	
419	All three modes keep the whole document in view. A cross-section hole is findable only when both
420	sides of the seam are present and named the same at review time. The new-surface review narrows the
421	findings to the new surface's seams, and the feature-fit review narrows them to the feature's fit.
422	The reading still covers the whole document.
423	
424	Where a design-consistency review follows this pass, it is keyed to these modes:
425	
426	- a full review, including a standalone "review the spec", draws the full design review;
427	- a surface add draws the scoped one;
428	- a feature-fit review draws the scoped one exactly when its second-sibling question answers yes, and
429	  draws none otherwise;
430	- a re-check at the pre-merge gate draws none, and the design review stands down there.
431	
432	**Reviewing a rewrite before it merges: judge the delta.** A restructure or a migration is gated for
433	merging back into the main line. That merge gate judges the delta. It has three parts:
434	
435	- load-bearing token identity, old text against new, modulo the per-chunk named deltas, plus a
436	  punctuation-multiset check that catches a restructure which preserved every word and changed the
437	  sentence boundaries.
438	
439	  A load-bearing token is one word of the document's content, with markup and whitespace left out. A
440	  chunk is one stretch of the old document the restructure moved as a unit. A named delta is a change
441	  the restructure's own record declared for that chunk in advance.
442	
443	  Produce the comparison this way. Build the word-token multiset of the old text and of the new. Build
444	  the punctuation multiset of each, since word-token identity alone passes a reflow that moved
445	  punctuation. Set the named deltas aside, and compare each pair. Two runs of this gate must agree, so
446	  write down the command or the script the project used and keep it with the gate's record. This skill
447	  ships no such script. Where the project has none either, say so in the record and read the gate's
448	  token part as not runnable;
449	- the full test suite green on the merged tree;
450	- a full review pass on both sides, whose blocking set is scoped to the delta.
451	
452	Four things block: an unmatched token, a red suite, a finding present on the new side and absent on
453	the old side. A meaning change nobody named blocks too. The pass reads the old tree and the merged
454	tree. A finding present on both is pre-existing, and a finding new to the merged side is delta-scoped.
455	Pre-existing findings become tracked follow-ups in the same change and never block, so the merge
456	stands free of debts it did not create.
457	
458	This gate runs where both sides are in reach. A document handed over on its own carries no old side.
459	The gate then stands down by name, and the pass reads the document as it stands.
460	
461	The token-identity part applies to a restructure meant to preserve content. A deliberate redesign
462	changes content by intent. Its merge stands on the green suite and the delta-scoped review pass,
463	with no token-identity demand over text the redesign meant to change.
464	
465	**The interpretation rule.** The author may state a standard out loud. Where the review sharpens it
466	past the words they used, state the sharpened form back to them, and mark it as the reviewer's own
467	reading. A standard nobody stated is never applied as though they had stated it.

469	## Phase 0 — Triage
470	
471	Before any analysis, decide whether the input is suitable.
472	
473	Check:
474	- Is this a product spec, feature doc, HLD, LLD, or design proposal?
475	- Does it describe a system with state, behavior, transitions, rather than marketing copy, vision
476	  statements, or prose with no operational content?
477	- Is there enough material to extract a model?
478	- **Does the document claim to describe a shipped system?** Then require pins: each surface naming
479	  the `file:line` that carries it. With the pins absent, every finding is conditional on the document
480	  being current. Say so, and flag any section describing a surface with no owning code or test as
481	  possibly-removed. A spec that outran a deletion will otherwise "prove" dead behaviour. Where the
482	  code is out of reach altogether, say that in one line. This happens when the document arrived on
483	  its own, or when the repository is elsewhere. Mark every finding on the already-built parts
484	  conditional, and review the document as written.
485	- **Is the input an architecture document?** That is valid input, and the review runs with the
486	  **architecture lens**. It holds seven checks, each judged at the scale the project's own kind sets.
487	  The project states its kind in a few words. Examples: a backend service, a static site, a fullstack
488	  app, a command-line tool, and a mobile app. Others: a library, a data pipeline, a skill pack, or a
489	  book. Any other kind is stated the same way. The kind decides the form each check can demand, so a skill pack and a backend
490	  service answer the placement check differently. The seven checks:
491	  - Every fact the requirements document states is owned by exactly one node.
492	  - No node stands without backing in the requirements. A node with one caller and no promised second
493	    is flagged as speculative. It waits for an answer: a named plan that turns it into a yes, or
494	    a merge back into its caller. Three questions decide whether a node stands on its own. Can it be
495	    tested by itself? Does a real second place need it? Can it and its neighbour be worked on at the
496	    same time without queuing on the same files? One "no" calls for an answer before the node stands,
497	    and the speculative-node case above is one of those. Two or more reads the node as premature.
498	  - Every seam names what crosses it and which side owns the format.
499	  - The quality budgets are stated with the place each number is measured, and each names its
500	    watcher. The watcher is the mechanical check that fails past the stated number. A decided
501	    sentence naming why a person reads a budget by eye is the other form the watcher takes.
502	  - The runtime view walks every flow the requirements promise.
503	  - The placement view says where every node runs, with its load-bearing technology where one exists.
504	  - The node-growth re-ask. Each node re-answers the three fitness questions on its pins as they
505	    stand now, because a node born right and then grown carries a standing yes nobody re-reads.
506	    Co-residence in one file is the mechanical face of a failed growth answer. Read the node count
507	    per file from this document's own pin column, counting the distinct nodes whose pins name a
508	    file. Raw file size is the wrong signal for this. A file holding more than one node is read for
509	    whether its co-resident nodes each still earn their place. Record the per-file node counts with
510	    the review. That count is a ceiling: the next review reads any file whose count rose as a question
511	    about what grew. A split moves through the architecture step and its re-review.
512	
513	  Every pin is a real `file:line` citation, and a prose description fails that bar. The paired
514	  requirements document must be in view, because ownership is checkable only against the fact list it
515	  owns. Where no such document exists, ask the author for it. Where none can be produced, record
516	  the ownership check as not runnable with that reason, and run the remaining six.
517	
518	Output one of:
519	
520	`TRIAGE: PROCEED` — analyzable. State a one-line reason. Continue to the opening assessment and Phase
521	1 in this same response, with no pause.
522	
523	`TRIAGE: NEEDS_CLARIFICATION` — the document carries too little operational content. List 2–4
524	observations, then 2–3 sharp clarifying questions. Stop there and wait.
525	
526	`TRIAGE: WRONG_ARTIFACT` — a vision deck, marketing copy, a pitch, or similar. State that plainly.
527	Offer to outline what the document would need to specify to become analyzable. Stop there.
528	
529	## Opening assessment
530	
531	Right after a `PROCEED`, give the author your one-paragraph view — what you'd say in the first 30
532	seconds of a review meeting.
533	
534	Cover:
535	- What this design is trying to do, in one sentence.
536	- The biggest 1–2 things working in this document.
537	- The biggest 1–2 things that need attention.
538	- Overall confidence: ready to build, needs another iteration, needs significant rework, or unclear
539	  yet.
540	
541	5–8 sentences. If the design is mostly solid, say so. If it has serious problems, state that plainly.
542	Then proceed to Phase 1.
543	
544	## Phase 1 — The model
545	
546	Extract the system's structural model.
547	
548	1a. Entities and their relationships.
549	1b. States and transitions for each entity that has a lifecycle.
550	1c. Actors — who initiates each significant action.
551	1d. Composition and boundaries if multiple components.
552	
553	For each, produce a prose list. Render a visual diagram only if the trigger conditions apply.
554	
555	Then add a short subsection titled "What I assumed":
556	- Where the document was ambiguous and you read it one way.
557	- What you treated as out-of-scope based on context.
558	- Which entities or actors you had to infer.
559	
560	This subsection tells the author the foundation on which the property analysis sits. They can correct
561	any wrong assumption after seeing the full review.
562	
563	Continue to Phase 2 in the same response.
564	
565	## Phase 2 — Structural issues in the model
566	
567	Find structural problems with the model itself, independent of any specific safety or liveness
568	property.
569	
570	Look for:
571	- Incomplete state space: hidden parameters (version, mode, tier), edge cases mentioned in passing,
572	  external dependencies whose state matters.
573	- Undefined or ambiguous actors.
574	- Composition issues: components mixing roles (a coordinator that also acts), unclear ownership.
575	- Abstraction problems: case-by-case rules that should be one general property, or abstract claims
576	  hiding critical distinctions.
577	
578	Write findings using the four-part format. After findings, re-render the relevant diagram with gaps
579	marked if a diagram was rendered. Continue to Phase 3.
580	
581	## Phase 3 — Property analysis
582	
583	For every entity, transition, and operation, check whether the document specifies the right
584	properties.
585	
586	3a. Things that must never happen (safety):
587	- Missing invariants: properties that must hold across all operations yet go unstated.
588	- Missing preconditions and postconditions.
589	- Atomicity: multi-step operations described as single actions; observable intermediate states;
590	  failure between steps.
591	- Rollback: what state the system returns to on failure.
592	
593	3b. Things that must eventually happen (liveness):
594	- Dead-end states: states with no defined exit.
595	- Termination: async operations, retries, migrations — is eventual completion guaranteed? Timeout,
596	  fallback, circuit breaker?
597	- Silent failure masking: can a successful event silently overwrite a previous failure?
598	
599	3c. Whether the spec can actually be enforced:
600	- Spec-model mismatch: properties promised but unenforceable in the underlying system.
601	- Counterexamples: for each non-trivial property, can you construct a sequence that breaks it?
602	
603	3d. Internal consistency:
604	- Contradicting requirements that can't simultaneously hold.
605	- Spec-model contradictions: behavior specified that no actor or transition supports.
606	- Overlapping-data agreement: sometimes two clauses independently describe overlapping data, such as
607	  a count here and the counted contents there, or a list in one section and its length in another. Is
608	  their agreement stated as an invariant? Two homes for one derivable fact with no tying sentence
609	  drift apart, and the tie is the finding's proposed sentence.
610	
611	3e. Generative stress-testing — three tiers: mandatory sweeps, imaginative probes, and the class
612	lens standing alone.
613	
614	**Open `reference/stress-lenses.md` now, and read it before writing a single Phase 3e finding.** That
615	file sits in this skill's own directory, beside this one. It carries all three tiers in full: the
616	five mandatory sweeps, the imaginative probes, and the class lens. Running Phase 3e from memory
617	skips the sweeps, and the record then reads as a full pass that never ran them.
618	
619	The sweeps' questions and the probes' full text live in that file alone. The mode list above names
620	them; only the file states what each one asks.
621	
622	Stress-test every operation, transition, rule, and assumption against the families of questions the
623	file holds. The specific cases are yours to invent, from what the operation actually does.
624	
625	The tiers differ in what they owe. `reference/stress-lenses.md` states what each tier owes, beside
626	the lenses themselves, and this page keeps no second copy of it.
627	
628	For any given operation, one or two lenses produce a real finding, and the rest read obviously fine.
629	That is expected, and the work is in the imagining. Each axis owes a finding only where one is real.
630	A mandatory sweep owes its verdict line even at a finding count of zero, and that is what "clean"
631	says. A lens that prompts no real concern produces no finding, and inventing an issue to satisfy a
632	lens is forbidden.
633	
634	Write findings using the four-part format.
635	
636	After findings, render three coverage tables in pipe-separated markdown:
637	
638	CRUD coverage per entity: | Entity | Create | Read | Update | Delete | Notes | — mark each cell
639	covered/partial/missing.
640	Invariants per state: | State | Invariants stated | Invariants missing |
641	Authorization per action: | Action | Roles allowed | Granular check enforceable? | Notes |
642	
643	Sometimes every row of a table would read N/A for this product. Authorization does that for a
644	single-user local tool, and so does create-read-update-delete where the product holds no user-mutated
645	persistent entities. Replace that table with one line saying so and why, because a table full of N/A
646	is ritual noise that trains the author to skim.
647	
648	Every full review also renders the surface × sweep verdict table, whatever the three tables above did.
649	Surfaces run down the side, the mandatory sweeps across, and each cell reads hit / clean /
650	N/A-with-reason. One verdict fills each cell, meaning one per sweep per surface. Where the document
651	lists no surfaces, the table collapses to a single row, and each sweep owes one verdict in it.
652	That keeps a skipped sweep distinguishable from a sweep that found nothing. On a
653	document where all three tables above go N/A, this table is the only coverage artifact the review
654	leaves behind. A screen-interaction spec and a read-only reporting tool are two such documents. The
655	shape, with one row per surface whatever kind the surfaces are:
656	
657	| Surface | Cross-cutting laws | Edge conditions | Policy uniformity | Lifecycle | Unwritten seams |
658	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
659	| `POST /orders` | clean | hit (F3) | hit (F5) | clean | clean |
660	| Checkout page | clean | hit (F4) | hit (F5) | hit (F7) | clean |
661	
662	Then write the class line beneath that table. One of three shapes carries it:
663	
664	- `Class lens: swept — <the classes filed>`, where a defect was found and its look-alikes swept. The
665	  line names each class the review filed.
666	- `Class lens: no class`, where the review read the whole document and found no class to file. A
667	  review that found no defect at all writes this line too.
668	- `Class lens: N/A — <reason>`, where the review could not read the whole document, so no sweep for
669	  look-alikes was open to it. The reason names what stood out of view.
670	
671	Continue to Phase 3.5.
672	
673	## Phase 3.5 — Acknowledged gaps
674	
675	Surface the gaps the document itself flags, in the four shapes listed under "Hidden gaps vs
676	acknowledged gaps" above. Each one gets a short note in the same four-part shape, written as
677	commentary on a known issue. The headline restates the open question in plain words. Part 3 gives the
678	second-order consequence the author may not have spelled out. Part 4 recommends one or two specific
679	options with tradeoffs, and your preference where you hold one.
680	
681	End with: `acknowledged · plain-label (formal-term)`.
682	
683	Where the document flags no gaps, write "No explicit Open Items or TBDs in the document." and move
684	on. Continue to Phase 4.
685	
686	## Phase 4 — Human and operational factors
687	
688	Properties that resist formal checking but matter equally:
689	
690	- Human observability: can operators understand the system's state? Are identifiers readable? Are
691	  errors actionable?
692	- Domain language on every surface: the words the product hands out speak the product's own
693	  vocabulary. An internal identifier, a code, and a mechanism name each stay out of them. Three shapes
694	  to catch: a card labelled with a developer tag, and an error body returning an internal enum name. A
695	  third is a command printing a class name at the user. Extract the strings the document promises to emit,
696	  wherever they land, and read them as the recipient would; a leaked internal word is a finding.
697	- Cognitive load: mode-dependent behavior, exceptions, special cases users must remember.
698	- Operational UX: debuggability, audit trails, traceability.
699	- Performance and scale budgets: how big can the input get in size, count, and duration before the
700	  artifact is unusable? State the assumed ceiling explicitly.
701	- Security and privacy: where they are genuinely out of scope for this product, name that as an
702	  explicit skip. A silent blind spot fails this bar.
703	
704	Use the four-part finding format. The same concreteness test applies: describe what the operator
705	actually does, and what they can actually observe when it goes wrong. A vague claim such as "operators
706	may be confused" fails it.
707	
708	Continue to Phase 5.
709	
710	## Phase 5 — Closing summary
711	
712	Open the summary with one line naming this skill and the version from this file's metadata, so a
713	record kept from the review says which prover produced it.
714	
715	Six short blocks:
716	
717	1. Top 3 things to fix before development. Reference finding IDs. One line each.
718	2. Properties the document should state explicitly, in plain language. Phrase each one so the author
719	   pastes it straight in. Two examples. "Every Failed state has a guaranteed path to either Updated
720	   or Reverted". "The sum of allocated units across all groups equals the total count of active
721	   units".
722	3. Open questions where you genuinely need author input — only those that cannot be resolved by
723	   inspection.
724	4. Recommendations queued for a judgment call. These are the findings labelled `recommendation`,
725	   where everything stated holds and a consistency or quality gain is on offer. List them so the
726	   author weighs each one, apart from the defects that get applied first.
727	5. On a full review only: the count of provisional-default sentences accumulated in the document,
728	   with the oldest 5 listed for a judgment call. A provisional-default mark carries no date, so read
729	   oldest as document order: the five marks standing earliest in the document. Every lens may close
730	   on a provisional default, and nothing else ever sweeps them. Without this line, most of a
731	   document's sentences can end up as values nobody approved, while every review still reports no
732	   findings.
733	6. What holds. One line for each strength that survived the whole pass, two or three at most. Skip
734	   this block where the pass found none.
735	
736	Where it helps clarity, render a coverage tree as a real visual diagram. Skip it where the textual
737	summary already conveys the picture.
738	
739	Finish with one sentence on overall readiness: ready to build / needs another iteration / needs
740	significant rework.
741	
742	In the conversation, render this summary first, followed by the three expanded findings and the
743	compact index. The record keeps the phase order and full evidence; the author does not need a second
744	copy of it in chat.
745	
746	## Meta rules
747	
748	- Claims about the shipped system rest on primary sources: `file:line` citations you actually
749	  resolved, and a command's output you actually ran. The document's own prose backs no such claim,
750	  and a summary of the document backs none either.
751	- Phase pacing: a `PROCEED` triage → opening assessment → Phase 1 → 2 → 3 → 3.5 → 4 → 5, all in one
752	  continuous pass, with no pause. The persisted record carries that full order. The conversation
753	  uses the compact decision layer defined above.
754	- When a fix a finding proposed is applied to the document, re-read the changed part. A fix can
755	  introduce a new gap, and the re-read is where that gap gets caught.
756	
757	## Persisting the record
758	
759	Write the findings to a dated file in the project under review. The default path is
760	`docs/review/YYYY-MM-DD.md`, and a path the user names wins over it. A document reviewed
761	outside any project gets its record beside the document itself. Each finding carries its kind, defect or recommendation, and a column
762	recording whether it was applied or rejected with the reason. That makes the outcome verifiable after
763	memory is gone, and it lets the next run check the previous run's unapplied rows.
764	
765	The record opens by naming the version of this skill that ran the pass. It also records the first 12
766	characters of the SHA-256 digest of `SKILL.md` and `reference/stress-lenses.md`, labelled separately.
767	A later session then tells whether a "recently reviewed" document used the current lens set or an
768	older one. A review method that grew a lens re-arms the full pass over documents reviewed under the
769	older set.
770	
771	A full review pass's record carries the mandatory-sweep verdict table beside the findings, in the
772	shape Phase 3e states.
773	
774	**For whoever sets up the project's records.** The project may run other review passes that also
775	write dated records. Give them all one shared shape, so a later reader reads each pass's outcome the
776	same way. Records written before that shape was agreed stay as they are.
777	
778	**A note for whoever maintains this skill.** This applies when a new release of the skill is being
779	prepared; a review in progress is unaffected. Before releasing a version of this skill, run one
780	adversarial pass over it from a clean context. It should be a fresh session, held by someone who
781	authored none of that release's changes. Where the release grew a new
782	lens or rule, run that lens against this skill's own body and name the result in the release's record.
783	A count-versus-contents lens then catches its own miscount, and a reading-load lens its own dense
784	bullet.
785	
786	## Glossary mode
787	
788	Triggers: a request written in plain English inside a message — "glossary", "glossary liveness",
789	"define atomicity", "what does liveness mean?". The same words after a leading slash count too.
790	
791	No command is registered anywhere for these words. A message that opens with a slash reaches Claude
792	Code's own command picker, so the working form is ordinary text.
793	
794	For a single term, output three things. A one-sentence plain definition. A one-sentence example,
795	taken from the document where possible. And the question this concept prompts you to ask in design
796	review.
797	
798	Example for a request about liveness:
799	**liveness** — a property that says something good must eventually happen. Example: a failed state
800	should eventually retry, succeed, or roll back; a state with no exit is a liveness violation. What to
801	ask: for every state, can the entity get out of it?
802	
803	For a glossary request naming no term, list every formal term used so far in this session, one-sentence
804	definitions only.
805	
806	Definitions to use (keep these exact, and paraphrase none of them loosely):
807	- **state-space** — the set of all situations the system can be in.
808	- **transitions** — the moves between states.
809	- **actors** — who initiates an action: user, role, automated service, external system.
810	- **composition** — how separate components combine. Clean when components have sharp roles.
811	- **abstraction** — replacing case-by-case enumeration with a general rule.
812	- **invariant** — a property that must hold across every reachable state.
813	- **precondition** — what must be true before an action runs.
814	- **postcondition** — what must be true after an action completes.
815	- **atomicity** — an operation either completes fully or leaves no trace.
816	- **rollback** — what the system reverts to on failure.
817	- **safety** — the family of properties meaning "nothing bad ever happens".
818	- **liveness** — the family of properties meaning "something good eventually happens".
819	- **dead-end** — a state with no defined exit.
820	- **discharge** — actually proving (or implementing) a property using the system's primitives.
821	- **consistency** — whether the spec's stated rules can all simultaneously hold.
822	- **contradiction** — two stated rules that openly conflict.
823	- **observability** — whether operators can see and understand the system's state.
824	- **cognitive-load** — mental effort users spend tracking modes, exceptions.
825	- **ops-ux** — operational UX: debuggability, audit trails, traceability.
826	
827	Glossary requests are standalone. Answer them without re-running the review.
828	
829	---
830	
831	Made with [live-spec](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec), the fuller method this skill was
832	lifted from. This is edition `1.2.0-standalone`: it carries its own version and follows no live-spec
833	release.
834	
835	---
836	
837	made with [live-spec](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec) v4.3.0
